cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why is Fino fortified to about 15% and Oloroso to about 17%?
cards.a: Flor yeast survives only to roughly 15.5% abv. Below that the flor layer lives and shields the wine from oxygen: biological ageing, which gives Fino its saline, bready character. Above it the flor dies and the wine ages oxidatively, giving Oloroso its nutty, dried-fruit profile.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why does a large diurnal temperature range help red wine quality?
cards.a: Warm days drive photosynthesis and phenolic ripening, and the berry burns off malic acid faster as it warms. Cool nights slow that loss, so the fruit gains sugar and colour while holding acidity. Trials suggest the night alone matters less than the season's warmth.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Malolactic conversion always softens acidity. So why does it not always taste buttery?
cards.a: It converts sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, raising pH. Diacetyl, the buttery compound, is only a by-product: the bacteria can metabolise it further, lees stirring disperses it, and blending dilutes it. Chablis, in northern Burgundy, routinely does MLF without tasting buttery.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A bottle says Spätlese. Is the wine sweet?
cards.a: Not necessarily. Prädikat levels measure must weight, the sugar in the grapes at harvest, not residual sugar in the finished wine. A Spätlese can be fermented bone dry and labelled Spätlese Trocken.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Where does the biscuit and brioche character in Champagne come from?
cards.a: Autolysis. The second fermentation happens inside the bottle, and the dead yeast cells then break down in contact with the wine under pressure. Tank-method wines finish their second fermentation in a pressurised tank with little lees contact, so they keep primary fruit and florals instead.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: What does Gran Reserva actually guarantee?
cards.a: Only maturation. For reds: at least 60 months in total, of which a minimum of 24 in oak and 24 in bottle. It says nothing about vineyard site or fruit quality. A producer can bottle an outstanding wine as Genérico if they choose to age it differently.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Someone calls a wine firm. How do you work out whether they mean acid or tannin?
cards.a: Acid is a taste. You register it at the sides of the tongue and it makes you salivate. Tannin is tactile: it binds salivary proteins and leaves the mouth dry. A high-acid, low-tannin Riesling and a low-acid, high-tannin red both feel firm, for opposite reasons.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why would a winemaker choose fourth-fill barrels that impart almost no flavour?
cards.a: For texture rather than flavour. The extractable oak compounds are largely spent, but the barrel still allows slow oxygen ingress, which polymerises tannin and stabilises colour. Neutral oak is a deliberate tool, not a compromise.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Two growers bottle Chambertin Grand Cru. Why can the wines differ so much?
cards.a: Because Burgundy classifies land, not producers. Le Chambertin is one vineyard divided among many owners, each with their own parcels, viticulture and winemaking. The classification guarantees the site; it says nothing about the execution.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why does vintage matter far more in Chablis than in the Languedoc, at opposite ends of France?
cards.a: Chablis sits at the northern margin of viable Chardonnay, where spring frost and poor flowering weather regularly threaten both crop size and ripeness. Warm, dry regions ripen reliably every year, so the differences between vintages are much smaller.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A technically dry wine reads as slightly sweet. What is happening?
cards.a: Ethanol itself tastes faintly sweet at moderate concentration, and glycerol adds body, so high-alcohol dry wines can read off-dry. Where acidity is too low to balance that alcohol, the same wine reads hot instead.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A label says old vine. What does that guarantee?
cards.a: Almost nothing. The term is unregulated in most of the world. The underlying mechanism is real: lower vigour, smaller yields, and deep roots that buffer drought. But with no legal minimum age it stays a claim rather than a specification.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Port is not back-sweetened. So why is it sweet?
cards.a: The ferment is stopped early. Neutral grape spirit goes in at around 6–8% abv and kills the yeast while a large amount of grape sugar is still unfermented. The sweetness is leftover must, not an addition.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Grapes contain both tartaric and malic acid. Why does tartaric matter more to the winemaker?
cards.a: It is the stronger and far more stable of the two, and it largely survives fermentation and ageing. Malic is respired away by the vine in warm conditions and can be converted by MLF. Tartaric is what ultimately underpins the finished wine's pH.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: What does the word oolong actually specify?
cards.a: A processing range, not a plant and not a place. Oxidation spans roughly 20–80%, the widest of any category. Anxi tieguanyin, from southern Fujian, sits near 20% and close to green tea; Wuyi yancha, northern Fujian, runs 50–70% plus charcoal roast and sits close to black.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: What is the difference between oxidation and roasting?
cards.a: Oxidation is enzymatic and happens to the fresh leaf: it is the process that turns green tea into black. Roasting is applied heat after processing is finished: it caramelises sugars and drives off moisture, and it can be repeated years later to revive a stored tea.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: How do sheng and shou puerh differ?
cards.a: Not by age. By process. Sheng is pressed raw and transforms slowly over decades. Shou was developed in the 1970s to imitate that result using 45–60 days of wet piling, wo dui, an accelerated microbial fermentation. Five-year examples of each have very little in common.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why is Taiwanese high-mountain oolong so much less astringent?
cards.a: Above roughly 1000m, cooler temperatures and persistent cloud slow the plant's growth and reduce catechin production, while amino acids stay relatively higher. Catechins are the main source of astringency. The result reads thick and sweet rather than brisk.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: What is yan yun, and what is it attributed to?
cards.a: Rock rhyme: the mineral signature of Wuyi yancha, off the cliffs of northern Fujian. It is credited to the weathered volcanic and sandstone soils of the narrow ravines, with sharp drainage and little direct sun. Zhengyan, true cliff tea, costs many times the flat-land tea.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why does Chinese green tea taste nutty while Japanese green tea tastes marine?
cards.a: The fixing method. China pan-fires, which introduces Maillard character: chestnut, toast, a rounder body. Japan steams, which halts oxidation faster and preserves more chlorophyll, producing the vivid green, grassy, oceanic profile of sencha and gyokuro.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why does white tea keep developing in storage when green tea merely goes stale?
cards.a: White tea is only withered and dried. There is no fixing step, so its enzymes are never fully deactivated and slow transformation continues. Aged Shou Mei is a recognised category. Green tea's enzymes are killed during fixing, so it can only degrade.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why does gongfu brewing taste different from Western brewing of the same leaf?
cards.a: It is a different extraction curve. A high leaf-to-water ratio with very short steeps pulls compounds out in stages, so you taste the tea evolve across infusions. A single long Western steep extracts most of it at once, averaging that whole progression into one cup.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Is the jade-green, intensely floral style of tieguanyin, Anxi's famous oolong, the traditional one?
cards.a: No. It is a market development from around the 1990s. Traditional tieguanyin, from Anxi in southern Fujian, was more oxidised, near 40%, and roasted. Demand for green, aromatic oolong pushed producers to 15–30% oxidation with little or no roast. Both are true to their era.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Which tea should not be stored airtight, and why?
cards.a: Sheng puerh. Green, white and oolong all degrade with oxygen, light and humidity, so they want a seal. Sheng needs modest airflow and humidity for its microbial and oxidative ageing to proceed at all. Sealed away, it simply stalls.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why does the same leaf taste different at home than it did in the shop?
cards.a: Usually the water rather than the tea. Mineral content changes both extraction and aroma perception: hard water mutes delicate aromatics and flattens greens, while very soft water can leave a tea tasting thin. Most specialists target low to moderate mineralisation.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: What is withering actually for?
cards.a: Controlled moisture loss. It makes the leaf pliable enough to roll without shattering, and it starts the chemical changes that precede oxidation. Under-withered leaf breaks up during processing; over-withered leaf loses aromatic potential before it is even rolled.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Madeira, the fortified wine from a Portuguese island out in the Atlantic, is deliberately heated in production. What does that heating buy?
options: It kills the yeast, which is what stops fermentation
It makes the wine effectively indestructible once opened
It concentrates the sugars by driving off water
It takes the harshness off the fortifying spirit
cards.a: The wine is cooked on purpose, oxidised and caramelised before it is ever sold. Because that damage has already been done deliberately, air and time can do very little more to it: an open bottle keeps for months where a table wine keeps days. The heating is estufagem.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why is the Left Bank of Bordeaux planted to Cabernet Sauvignon and the Right Bank to Merlot?
options: The Left Bank was replanted to Cabernet after phylloxera
The 1855 classification requires a Cabernet majority
The Left Bank is simply the warmer of the two
Gravel drains fast and holds heat; clay stays cool and damp
cards.a: Soil, not latitude. The Left Bank's deep gravel drains hard and stores heat, which late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon needs to finish. Right Bank clay and limestone hold water and stay cooler, and Merlot buds and ripens early enough to cope with that.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Barolo is pale and browns young. Why is it also one of the most tannic wines made?
options: A long maceration pulls out tannin but bleaches the colour
The pigment fades in barrel while the oak adds the tannin
Nebbiolo is poor in pigment and extremely rich in tannin
It is picked before the skins colour, to protect the acidity
cards.a: Colour and grip are different compounds, and a grape can be short of one and loaded with the other. Nebbiolo has little anthocyanin and what it has is unstable, so it goes orange at the rim early. Depth of colour tells you nothing about structure.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: What actually separates the Northern from the Southern Rhône?
cards.a: Grape and terrain. In the north Syrah is the only black grape permitted, worked on steep granite terraces in a continental climate. The south is Mediterranean, flatter and many times larger, and its reds are Grenache-led blends where no one variety carries the wine.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: How does one Loire grape make bone dry, sweet and sparkling wine equally well?
cards.a: Chenin Blanc holds very high acidity even when fully ripe, so sugar never reads as flabby and the base wine is taut enough for sparkling untouched. Thin skins take botrytis readily, and bunches ripen unevenly, which is why the sweet wines are picked in several passes.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A corked wine smells of damp cardboard. What else has the taint done to it?
options: Blunted your sense of smell, so the wine's own aroma is muted
Oxidised the wine, which is why the fruit has gone
Bound to the tannin, leaving the finish hard and short
Raised the volatile acidity, adding a vinegar edge
cards.a: TCA does not only add a musty smell, it suppresses olfactory signalling, so it takes aroma away as well. A lightly tainted bottle reads as dull and fruitless rather than obviously faulty, which is the version most people pour and blame on the wine.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: What does serving a tannic red too cold actually do to it?
cards.a: Cold raises the perception of acidity and bitterness, tannin included, and slows the release of aromatic compounds. Warmth does the reverse and pushes alcohol forward. So an over-chilled red reads hard and mute, and a warm one reads sweet and spirity.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why does a good red fall apart next to asparagus or a soft-boiled egg?
cards.a: Umami raises the perception of bitterness, astringency and acidity, so a tannic wine turns hard and hollow against it. Salt is the counterweight and does the opposite, softening tannin and acid, which is why seasoning the dish often rescues the pairing.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: What does a winemaker pay for including whole bunches in a red ferment?
cards.a: Stems buy aromatic lift, firmer tannin and a cooler, slower ferment. They also absorb pigment, so the wine finishes paler, and they release potassium, which raises pH at the cost of acidity. Unripe stems add a green, stalky note that never leaves.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why was Tignanello, from the heart of Chianti Classico, sold as Vino da Tavola?
options: It was aged in barriques, which the rules did not allow
The rules did not permit the blend it was made from
Its vineyard lay outside the delimited Chianti zone
It was declassified after failing the tasting panel
cards.a: Chianti then dictated the varieties and required a share of white grapes. Dropping them and adding Cabernet Sauvignon put the wine outside its own name, so it went out as table wine. A classification binds what you may blend, not only where you may pick.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: What decides which of the six classes a Chinese tea belongs to?
options: What was done to the leaf after picking, and in what order
The cultivar the leaf was picked from, and its variety
The colour of the dry leaf, and of the liquor it gives
The region it grew in and the altitude it grew at
cards.a: Processing alone. Green, yellow, white, oolong, red and dark all come from the same plant. Note the vocabulary too: what English calls black tea is hong cha, red tea, and dark tea is a separate class, the one that holds puerh and the other hei cha.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Kill-green is the burst of heat that shuts down the enzymes that would otherwise brown fresh leaf. Why is it a dial rather than a switch?
options: Because the leaf has to be dried at the same time
Because too much heat scorches the leaf and dulls it
Because every cultivar denatures at a different temperature
Because how much enzyme survives decides whether it can age
cards.a: Heat denatures the enzymes that drive oxidation, and how far it goes is a choice. Green tea is fixed hard, so nothing is left to change and it can only fade. Puerh's maocha, its unpressed loose leaf, is fixed gently and sun-dried, leaving enzyme and surface microbes intact for decades.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: What is rolling for, if the leaf is going to be oxidised anyway?
cards.a: It ruptures the cells so the enzymes and the compounds they act on finally meet, which is what lets oxidation run at all. It also sets the shape, and shape sets extraction: a tight ball opens over many infusions where broken leaf gives everything at once.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Black tea is often called fully fermented. Why is that the wrong word?
cards.a: Nothing microbial happens to it. Black tea is oxidised: the leaf's own enzymes react with its polyphenols in air, the chemistry that browns a cut apple. Real fermentation, microbes and all, belongs to the dark teas, and shou puerh's wet piling is the clearest case.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Yellow tea is made almost exactly like green tea. What is the extra step?
cards.a: Once the leaf is fixed it is wrapped warm and slightly damp for hours or days. The enzymes are already dead, so this is not oxidation: heat and moisture break chlorophyll down and soften the catechins, taking off the grassy edge. The step is men huang, sealed yellowing.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Two senchas come from one field and one was steamed far longer. Which is it?
options: The clear, sharp, aromatic one
The cloudy, sweet, thick one
The one that keeps its aroma longest in storage
The one that needs the longest infusion
cards.a: Deep steaming, fukamushi, runs a minute or more against roughly thirty seconds for light. The extra heat breaks the leaf apart, so fine particles cloud the cup, extraction is fast and sweet, astringency drops, and the aroma is quieter and keeps less well.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Gyokuro, the most prized Japanese green, is shaded for weeks before picking. What does the shade actually change?
options: It cools the leaf, which slows growth and concentrates sugar
It cuts the leaf's chlorophyll, and chlorophyll is what tastes grassy
It stops theanine being turned into catechins
It holds back the leaf's own aroma compounds
cards.a: Theanine is made in the roots and sent up to the leaf, where light drives its conversion toward catechins, the bitter compounds, and drives catechin synthesis besides. Take the light away for about three weeks and theanine builds up instead. That is the brothy weight.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Bud-only plucking is the finest grade, so why is oolong not picked that way?
cards.a: Different job. A bud is rich in theanine and caffeine, which suits a delicate green or a silver needle. Oolong wants kai mian cai, open-face picking of three or four mature leaves, because mature leaf holds the aroma precursors and survives long rolling and roasting.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: If every tea is one species, what does a cultivar name tell you?
options: The region it is legally allowed to be grown in
The class of tea it will be processed into
The age of the bush the leaf was picked from
The plant's chemistry, and so what it can be made into
cards.a: One species, sharply different clones. Var. assamica has large leaves and more polyphenol, var. sinensis is smaller and finer, and named cultivars go further still: Rou Gui, Qing Xin, Yabukita. Japan plants roughly 70% Yabukita, which narrows a whole country's flavour.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Phoenix Dancong, from the Fenghuang mountains in Guangdong, is sold by aroma name. Is anything added to make it smell that way?
cards.a: No. The names translate the smell: Mi Lan Xiang is honey orchid, Ya Shi Xiang is duck shit, and each is its own cultivar line off Fenghuang Shui Xian. Dan cong means single bush: the aromas were found on individual old trees, then propagated by cutting.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Oolong is sold as 20, 40 or 70 percent oxidised. What is that percentage a measurement of?
options: The share of the leaf's catechins that have reacted
The share of each leaf's surface that has browned
Nothing measured: it is the maker's estimate, by eye and nose
The share of the batch held back from the heat that stops it
cards.a: It is a convention rather than a reading. No maker measures the leaf in the moment; the figure is judged from the colour of the bruised margin, the smell and the feel, then passed on by habit. Two makers can call one tea 30% and 50%, so treat it as a style marker.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Mosel Riesling grows on steep slopes of dark slate. What is the slate mainly doing?
options: Passing its mineral flavour up into the wine
Holding water so the vines never run short
Storing the day's heat and giving it back at night
Raising the soil pH, which keeps acidity high
cards.a: Buying ripeness at the edge of where it is possible. At fifty degrees north the sun is low, so a steep slope meets it closer to square, and broken dark slate absorbs that heat and releases it overnight. The slatey note in the glass is a tasting term, not dissolved rock.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Unrolled oolong leaf comes out green in the middle with a red rim. What did that?
options: The roast scorching the thin edge of the leaf
The rim drying first and browning as it dries
Only the older leaves in the batch oxidising
Shaking the leaf until the edges bruise and oxidise
cards.a: Tossing the leaf in baskets or drums, resting it, and repeating that for hours. The tumbling bruises the margins and only the margins, so oxidation runs at the edge while the centre stays green. That is how oolong lands on a percentage instead of a switch. The step is yao qing.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One of these faults can genuinely improve in the glass. Which?
options: A corked bottle, once the taint has blown off
A wine that smells of struck match or rotten egg
A wine gone flat and brown before its time
A wine with a vinegar and nail polish edge
cards.a: Reduction: volatile sulfur compounds left by the yeast, which air can drive off, so a decant or a hard swirl often clears it. The other three are one-way. TCA, the trichloroanisole taint behind a corked bottle, oxidation and volatile acidity do not come back.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Matcha is ground leaf. What leaf, exactly, goes into the mill?
cards.a: Tencha. It is shaded like gyokuro and steamed like sencha, but it is never rolled, and the stems and veins are cut out before it dries flat. Rolling exists to shape leaf for infusing, and matcha is not infused, so the leaf goes to a stone mill whole.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Burgundy's crus rank vineyards. What does the 1855 classification rank?
options: The châteaux, at the prices their wines were fetching
The gravel banks of the Médoc, plot by plot
The estates, rechecked by a tasting panel every decade
The blend each property is permitted to make
cards.a: Properties, not plots. Brokers ranked the estates of the Médoc by what their wines sold for, and the rank has belonged to the name ever since. A classed growth that buys neighbouring land can bottle that fruit at its rank. A grand cru boundary cannot move.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Da Hong Pao, the most famous of the roasted Wuyi rock oolongs, is sold in every shop in northern Fujian. What is almost certainly in the bag?
options: Leaf from the six mother bushes on the cliff
A blend of Wuyi cultivars roasted to a house style
One named cultivar, the same one every year
Wuyi tea from the flat land below the cliffs
cards.a: Picking the mother bushes stopped in 2006, so nobody sells their leaf. Most Da Hong Pao is a blended roast of Wuyi cultivars, usually Shui Xian and Rou Gui, built to a house style. Qi Dan is a genuine cutting off the originals; Bei Dou tests as something else.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Germany's Prädikat ladder ranks ripeness. So how does a great vineyard get named?
cards.a: Separately, and by the growers first. The VDP, a private association, built a four-tier pyramid of origin topped by Grosse Lage, whose dry wine is bottled as Grosses Gewächs. The 2021 wine law copied that shape into statute, binding from 2026, though regions are still ranking sites.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why is gyokuro, a shaded Japanese green, brewed at around 60C when oolong takes boiling water?
options: Hot water scorches delicate leaf and makes it taste burnt
Cool water pulls the sweet amino acids and leaves the bitterness
The leaf is broken too finely to take water at full heat
Cool water slows extraction, so the leaf lasts more infusions
cards.a: Compounds do not all dissolve at the same temperature. Theanine and the other amino acids come out readily in cool water; catechins and caffeine need heat. Sixty degrees selects for sweetness and body. A tight oolong ball needs boiling water simply to open.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Ruby and tawny Port begin as the same wine. What actually separates them?
cards.a: Air. Tawny matures in seasoned casks small enough to let oxygen in, which fades the colour to amber and builds nut, fig and caramel. Ruby is held in large vats or tank with almost no air, keeping its purple and its fruit. Age follows from the vessel, not the reverse.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Two raw puerh cakes, same year and same processing, one Yiwu and one Bulang. How do they differ?
options: Yiwu is soft and honeyed, Bulang is bitter and powerful
Yiwu is the raw tea and Bulang the ripe one
Bulang is only stronger because it is picked later
They differ in how they were stored, not in the leaf
cards.a: Origin. Both are mountains in Xishuangbanna, southern Yunnan. Yiwu, east of the Mekong, gives a gentle, thick, honeyed tea; Bulang, west of it, is known for a bitterness that turns into huigan, the sweetness that floods back after you swallow. Lao Ban Zhang is Bulang's costliest village.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Traditional Rioja smells of coconut and sweet dill. Where does that come from?
options: The Tempranillo grape's own aromatics
A heavy toast level on the barrel
Years in bottle rather than in barrel
American oak, which is far richer in oak lactone
cards.a: The species of tree. American white oak carries much more cis oak lactone than French oak, and that single compound smells of coconut. Rioja bought American casks for generations, so a note that belongs to a forest reads as the signature of a region.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Shincha, sencha, bancha, kukicha: what do those names actually describe?
cards.a: When it was picked and which part of the plant it is, not a quality ladder. Shincha is the first flush of the year, sencha the standard rolled leaf, bancha a later and coarser picking, kukicha the stems sorted out during refining. Cheaper, and a different thing.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Where does the green pepper note in an underripe Cabernet come from?
options: Tannin from stems and seeds that never ripened
Malic acid, which runs high in unripe fruit
Methoxypyrazines, which sunlight and ripening break down
Yeast that struggles in a cold fermentation
cards.a: A compound the grape already holds. Methoxypyrazines smell of capsicum at vanishingly low concentrations, and they fall as the fruit ripens and the bunch sees sun. Cool sites, big crops and shaded canopies keep them, which is why growers strip leaves from the fruit zone.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: The same sheng cake is stored in Kunming and in Guangzhou. Which one changes faster?
options: Guangzhou, where the humidity is far higher
Kunming, because dry air draws the change out of the leaf
Neither: ageing tracks the leaf, not the room
Both alike, except that Guangzhou turns musty
cards.a: Humidity sets the rate. Guangzhou, on the subtropical south coast, sits above 80% much of the year, and a cake there darkens and softens in years rather than decades. Kunming, high in Yunnan, is cool and dry, so change is slow and clean. Push too far and you get mould.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why is Port fruit trodden or pumped so hard, and so early?
cards.a: The window is short. Fortifying at roughly half the sugar ends fermentation after about two days, and skin contact ends with it. All the colour and tannin the wine will ever have comes out inside that time. That is what a lagar is: a shallow granite trough to tread in.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Oriental Beauty is made from leaf that insects have already chewed. Why is that wanted?
options: The bites let oxidation begin out in the field
The insects only settle on the sweetest bushes
The plant answers the damage with honey-scented compounds
The damage forces a longer, slower withering
cards.a: The tea green leafhopper feeds on the young shoots and the plant answers chemically. Monoterpenes rise, the family behind muscat grapes and Darjeeling's muscatel note, and other compounds bring the honey. It is a wound response, so the field cannot be sprayed and yields fall.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: What is carbonic maceration doing that a normal red ferment is not?
cards.a: Fermenting the grape from the inside. Whole uncrushed berries are sealed under carbon dioxide, and each one starts converting its own sugar with its own enzymes, before yeast ever reaches it. That builds banana and kirsch esters, and takes colour without much tannin.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Two waters have the same hardness and one of them still flattens the tea. Why?
cards.a: Alkalinity: the bicarbonate in the water, measured separately from the calcium and magnesium that make it hard. Bicarbonate neutralises the tea's own acids and lifts the brew pH, so the liquor darkens and the aroma goes flat. Low alkalinity matters more than low hardness.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: The second fermentation leaves dead yeast inside the bottle. How does it get out?
cards.a: Riddling, then disgorgement. The bottle is tilted and turned until the sediment gathers in the neck, the neck is frozen, and the cap comes off so the pressure fires the plug clear. The gap is topped up with the dosage, and that sugar sets brut or demi-sec.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A white wine is left on its lees, the dead yeast left by fermentation, and stirred weekly. What does that buy?
options: A deeper colour, from pigment the yeast gives up
Higher acidity, because the lees hold on to malic acid
Texture, and some protection from oxygen
A faster finish, because the yeast is roused back to work
cards.a: Stirring the lees back through the wine. As the cells break down they release mannoproteins, which add weight and a creamy feel without any sugar. The lees also consume oxygen, so the wine is shielded. Overdone it buries the fruit. The French for the stirring is bâtonnage.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Alsace is one of France's most northerly wine regions. So why are its whites so ripe?
cards.a: The Vosges mountains take the rain out of the westerly weather, leaving Colmar among the driest towns in France. Sun and dry autumns push ripeness far, so an Alsace wine can be dry or distinctly sweet and taste ripe either way. Since 2021 an Alsace white must say which.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A bottle says Fleurie and the word Beaujolais appears nowhere on the label. What is it?
options: A Burgundy village that happens to lie near Beaujolais
One of the ten Beaujolais crus, each a name in its own right
Beaujolais Villages from the single village of Fleurie
A brand, since Fleurie is not a protected place name
cards.a: The top of three tiers: Beaujolais, Beaujolais Villages, then ten crus in the granite hills of the north, which carry only their own names. Granite gives firmer wine than the clay and sandstone of the flat south, so Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent can age where simple Beaujolais cannot.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Chablis has seven grand crus and they sit side by side on one hill. Why all in one place?
cards.a: Aspect, at the northern limit of ripe Chardonnay. That slope above the river Serein faces south west and takes the most sun in the region. It sits on Kimmeridgian marl, a clay and limestone packed with fossil oyster shells. Petit Chablis is mostly on younger rock above.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Almost no sherry carries a vintage. What is the system behind that?
options: A blend of several vintages chosen at bottling
A single cask topped up each year from the new harvest
Ageing so long that the vintage stops meaning anything
Continuous fractional blending down a stack of casks
cards.a: The solera. Casks sit in rows by age: a portion is drawn from the oldest row, the solera itself, which is refilled from the next youngest, a criadera, and so on up. Nothing is ever emptied, so young wine is folded into old for ever and age becomes an average.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Where does the petrol note in an older Riesling come from?
cards.a: TDN, a compound that builds in the bottle out of carotenoids, the pigments the grape uses to handle sunlight. Sun exposure, heat and water stress load the fruit with the precursors, which is why Australian Riesling can show petrol young and Mosel often never does.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Chianti Classico has three tiers. What does Gran Selezione require that Riserva does not?
options: A named single vineyard on the label
One hundred percent Sangiovese
Fruit from the producer's own vineyards
A minimum of three years in oak
cards.a: Estate fruit. Riserva may be made from bought grapes; Gran Selezione may not, and it ages thirty months against twenty four. From the 2027 harvest it also needs 90% Sangiovese and only Tuscan grapes beside it, so no Cabernet and no Merlot.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Nearly every wine has sulphur dioxide added. What is it actually doing?
cards.a: Two jobs: it stuns spoilage microbes, and it protects the wine from oxidation. Only the free portion works, since the rest binds to other compounds and goes inert. That is why a lab reports free and total separately, and why the total on its own tells you little.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Cork or screwcap. What is a bottle closure actually deciding?
options: How much oxygen reaches the wine, and how steadily
Whether the wine can age in bottle at all
How much wine is lost to evaporation over decades
Whether the bottle stays sterile
cards.a: Oxygen ingress, which is a dial and not a seal. A tin-lined screwcap admits almost nothing, keeping a wine fresh but leaving it liable to smell of struck match. Natural cork admits more, varies bottle to bottle, and carries the risk of cork taint.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A cool-climate grower adds sugar before fermentation and a warm-climate one adds acid. What is each fixing?
cards.a: Chaptalisation adds sugar to the juice so the yeast makes more alcohol. It does not sweeten the wine, because that sugar ferments away. Acidification adds tartaric acid to fruit that ripened too fast to keep its own. EU rules allow one or the other, never both.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A Taiwanese oolong is sold as Baozhong, Dong Ding, Alishan or Lishan. What does that name tell you?
options: The oxidation level, from lightest to heaviest
The roast, from none up to heavy charcoal
The cultivar, one for each mountain
Roughly where it sits on the island's elevation ladder
cards.a: Elevation, mostly. Baozhong comes from Pinglin at 400–800m, barely oxidised and left in loose twists rather than rolled into balls. Dong Ding sits at 600–800m and is traditionally roasted. Alishan begins around 1000m, Lishan at 1600m and above.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Oxidation turns green leaf into black tea. What does it do to catechins, the leaf's bitter compounds?
options: Caffeine, which is why black tea feels stronger
Sugars, which is where the malty sweetness comes from
Theaflavins first, then larger thearubigins
Tannins, the same compounds as in red wine
cards.a: Joins them up. Catechins pair off into theaflavins, which are orange, bright and brisk, and those link further into thearubigins, brown, soft and far more abundant, which carry the colour and the body. Stop the oxidation early for briskness, run it long for depth.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: What do gushu and taidi mean on a puerh label?
cards.a: Old tree and terrace. Gushu is leaf from old seed-grown trees standing in mixed forest; taidi is plantation tea, cloned, hedged low and picked often. Deep roots and small crops make gushu thicker and longer in the cup. Far more is sold as gushu than can exist.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Darjeeling is sold by flush. What is a flush, and why do the first two taste nothing alike?
cards.a: A flush is one growth cycle of the bush. First flush, from March, is barely oxidised and reads green and floral, closer to an oolong. Second flush, in May and June, is fully oxidised and gives the grapey muscatel note. Same bushes, different season, different making.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: What does CTC do to the leaf, and why is most Assam made that way?
cards.a: Crush, tear, curl: the leaf goes through toothed rollers that shred it into hard granules. Nearly every cell is broken, so oxidation is fast and complete and the brew is strong and dark in two minutes. It is built for milk, bags and one infusion, not for leaf grades.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: How does jasmine tea get its scent?
options: Fresh blossoms are layered through the leaf, then taken out again
Jasmine oil is sprayed onto the finished leaf before packing
Dried blossoms are blended into the leaf and left there
The bushes are grown among jasmine plants in the same field
cards.a: By absorption, repeated. Jasmine opens and releases its scent after dark, so the flowers are layered warm through the tea overnight, taken out, and replaced with fresh ones for up to nine rounds. Earl Grey is the other method: bergamot, a bitter citrus, applied to the leaf as an oil.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: White tea is called unprocessed. What actually happens to it?
cards.a: A long wither, one to three days, then a low drying. No heat is used to stop it and the leaf is never rolled, so a little oxidation creeps in anyway. The names are picking standards: Silver Needle is buds alone, Bai Mu Dan, white peony, a bud with a leaf or two.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why keep one pot of Yixing clay, from the potting town in Jiangsu, for one kind of tea?
options: The clay is porous and gives back what it has brewed before
The clay reacts with anything but the tea it was seasoned for
The pot is fired to suit one tea's brewing temperature
It is custom rather than anything the cup can taste
cards.a: The clay is fired unglazed and stays slightly porous, so oil and aroma soak into the wall and return to the next brew. Thick clay holds heat too, which suits roasted oolong and puerh. A porcelain gaiwan, the lidded cup, gives nothing back, so tasters judge in one.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Puerh is pressed into cakes. What does that do besides making it easy to carry?
cards.a: It slows the ageing and makes it even. Only the outside of a cake meets much air, so the whole piece changes together and more slowly than loose leaf, which ages faster and less evenly. Press it harder and it slows further: an iron-pressed cake outlasts a stone-pressed one.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc smells of passionfruit far louder than a Loire one. Where is that aroma made?
options: In the grape, which simply holds more of it in New Zealand
By long skin contact before the juice is fermented
By the yeast, cutting it free from odourless compounds in the juice
By fermenting cold enough to hold the volatiles in the wine
cards.a: In the ferment. The grape carries thiols, sulphur compounds smelling of passionfruit and grapefruit, but bound to amino acids where they have no smell at all. Yeast enzymes cut them loose, so the strain and the handling decide how much ever arrives.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Northern Rhône Syrah tastes of cracked black pepper and Barossa Shiraz almost never does. What decides that?
options: Cool, shaded ripening, which leaves the pepper compound intact
The stems, kept in the ferment in the north and removed in Australia
Granite soil, which the Barossa floor does not have
A different clone, selected in Australia for ripeness
cards.a: Rotundone, the compound that smells of black pepper. It builds late in ripening and only where the bunch stays cool and shaded; sun and heat break it down. Syrah and Shiraz are one grape, so what changes across the world is the temperature, not the vine.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Grenache ripens to very high sugar but makes pale, soft wine. Why is it so often blended?
cards.a: It brings alcohol, red fruit and a sweet texture, and not much else: low in pigment and tannin, and quick to oxidise. Syrah supplies colour and firmness, Mourvèdre tannin and savoury weight. The Southern Rhône blend is a structure the grape cannot build alone.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Chardonnay is called neutral. Why is that a reason to plant it rather than a complaint?
cards.a: It carries little aroma of its own, so what reaches the glass is site and cellar rather than grape: the same variety reads lean and stony in Chablis, at Burgundy's cold northern tip, and broad and buttery from a warm site fermented in barrel. It also ripens early almost anywhere.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Pinot Noir is called a difficult grape. What actually makes it difficult in the vineyard?
options: It ripens so late that only the warmest sites finish it
It needs limestone and sulks on any other soil
Thin skins in a tight bunch, and buds that break early
Its skins are so tannic that extraction has to be gentle
cards.a: Early budding puts it in the path of spring frost, and thin-skinned berries packed tightly together trap moisture and rot in a wet autumn. Those same thin skins give little pigment and little tannin, which is why the wine is pale and why nothing hides a mistake.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why does Bordeaux keep Cabernet Franc in the blend when Cabernet Sauvignon makes the bigger wine?
cards.a: Insurance and perfume. It buds and ripens a week or so earlier, so it finishes on cool, damp clay where Cabernet Sauvignon would stay green. It also brings lighter tannin and a violet lift. And it is the parent of both Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Napa Cabernet routinely finishes above 15% alcohol and Bordeaux rarely does. Why?
options: Napa may add sugar before fermentation and Bordeaux may not
Napa yeast strains ferment more of the sugar away
The fruit shrivels on the vine, which concentrates the sugar
Sugar arrives long before the tannins are ready, and the grower waits
cards.a: Sugar ripeness and phenolic ripeness, meaning the softening of tannin and the loss of green aromas, run on different clocks. In heat the sugar arrives first, so a grower who holds on for the tannin picks fruit already carrying 15% of potential alcohol. Hang time is bought with alcohol.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Argentina plants vines above 1000m and as high as 3000m. What does altitude buy besides cool nights?
cards.a: Ultraviolet light. The berry defends itself by loading its skin with anthocyanin, the colour pigment, and with tannin, so high-altitude Malbec comes out darker and firmer than the same grape grown low. The air is dry too, so almost every vine is irrigated from Andean snowmelt.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: The Barossa and Eden Valleys are neighbours in South Australia. Why is one known for Shiraz and the other for Riesling?
options: The Eden Valley has limestone where the Barossa floor has clay
The Eden Valley sits some 300m higher, so it ripens weeks later
The Eden Valley is nearer the coast and takes the sea breeze
Riesling was planted there first and the rules now protect it
cards.a: Height, not distance. Barossa vineyards sit around 250m and Eden Valley ones between roughly 380 and 550m, enough to slow ripening by one to three weeks. That late, cool finish holds the acidity Riesling needs, while the warm valley floor builds the Shiraz.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Chile re-cut its wine map east to west in 2011. What do Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes describe?
cards.a: How much cooling a site gets, rather than how far south it sits. Costa sits in reach of the cold Humboldt current off the Pacific. Andes takes night air draining off the mountains. Entre Cordilleras, between the ranges, is the warm central floor. A valley name hid all of it.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Hojicha is roasted brown and is drunk in the evening. Is the roasting what makes it low in caffeine?
cards.a: Only partly. Roasting at 150–200C drives some off, but most of it is the raw material: hojicha is made from bancha, the coarse late leaf, and from stems, both low in caffeine already. Genmaicha gets there differently, cutting the leaf with its own volume of roasted rice.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Sencha, kabusecha and gyokuro can be made from one field. What separates them?
options: How long the leaf is steamed once it comes off the bush
Which flush of the year the leaf was picked from
How finely the leaf is rolled before it is dried
How many days the bushes are covered, and how dark
cards.a: Shade, applied as two dials: how long, and how heavy. Sencha gets none. Kabusecha is covered for roughly a week to ten days, often with cloth laid straight over the bushes. Gyokuro runs twenty days or more under denser cover, so it goes furthest toward sweet and brothy.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A Ceylon pack says high grown. What does that actually tell you?
options: It is the top grade of that estate's crop
It was grown above 1200m, which makes it lighter and brisker
It is the top of the shoot, the bud and two leaves
It was grown in the hills, so it is stronger and darker
cards.a: Elevation, not rank. Sri Lanka splits its tea at 600m and 1200m. High grown, above 1200m, gives a pale, brisk, aromatic liquor. Low grown, under 600m, gives a dark, thick, heavy one that much of the Middle East prefers. Neither band is the better tea.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A Darjeeling tin is stamped FTGFOP. What is that grading?
options: The size and look of the dry leaf, and its bud content
The cup, as scored by a professional tea taster
The garden's rank in that season's auction
The flush it came from, first through to autumnal
cards.a: The leaf, not the liquor. The letters stack up a description: Orange Pekoe is a whole-leaf grade, and flowery, golden, tippy and finest each claim more bud or better appearance. None of it is a tasting score, and a broken grade can still brew the better cup.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why is the second infusion of a rolled oolong usually the strongest?
options: The water goes in hotter on the second pour than the first
The first infusion washes dust off the leaf
The bitter compounds only come out after the sweet ones
The leaf has opened, so far more of it now meets the water
cards.a: The first steep of a tight ball only wets the outside, and the leaf is still shut. By the second it has unfurled, so the water reaches every surface at once and the brew peaks. After that each steep takes what is left, and the tea thins and sweetens as it goes.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Darjeeling and Assam are sold by flush. Why is Kenyan tea never sold that way?
cards.a: It grows on the equator at 1500–2700m, so there is no winter and the bush never goes dormant. Leaf comes off every week or two all year, which leaves no first or second flush to name. Kenya is the largest exporter of black tea in the world and nearly all of it goes into blends.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why does milk soften a strong black tea?
options: Casein, the protein in milk, binds the tea's polyphenols
The fat coats the tongue and blocks the taste buds
It dilutes the brew, so there is less to taste
It cools the tea, and heat is what makes tannin harsh
cards.a: Astringency is polyphenols binding the proteins in your saliva and stripping the mouth dry. Milk brings its own protein, which binds them first, so less of that grip ever reaches you. The same trade is why a fatty dish softens a brisk tea and why dark tea suits rich meat.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A brick of Hunan dark tea is speckled with gold. What is that?
cards.a: A fungus, grown into the brick on purpose. The tea is pressed loose enough to breathe, then held warm and damp until it blooms right through. It softens coarse leaf and gives Fu brick its sweet, mushroomy smell. The name is golden flowers, and puerh is not the only dark tea.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: After a bitter, astringent tea, two separate things happen in the mouth. What are they?
cards.a: Two halves of one aftertaste. The mouth waters back after the tea has dried it, which is sheng jin, generating fluid. Then a sweetness rises in the throat as the bitterness fades: hui gan, returning sweetness. Bitterness is the trigger, not a fault.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Almost every vine in the world is two plants joined at the base. Why?
options: A root-feeding louse from America, which American roots survive
It holds the vine's vigour down and keeps the yield low
It lets a grower switch variety without replanting the vineyard
A leaf-eating pest that American vine leaves shrug off
cards.a: Phylloxera, an aphid that eats roots. It reached Europe in the 1860s and killed the European vine, whose roots cannot wall off the damage, while American species grew up with it and can. So European fruiting wood is grafted onto American roots. Chile, isolated and sandy, never had to.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: What does noble rot, a fungus deliberately welcomed onto ripe grapes, add that simply leaving them to shrivel does not?
options: Higher alcohol, since the fungus ferments some of the sugar
Sweetness, because drying alone concentrates only the acid
Aromas the grape never had: honey, dried apricot, saffron
Deeper colour, from the browning it causes in the skin
cards.a: Concentration is the easy half: the fungus pierces the skin, water evaporates out, and sugar and acid both climb. The rest is its own chemistry, which builds notes no raisined grape carries. It wants misty mornings and dry afternoons; left wet, the same fungus ruins the crop as grey rot.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One rosé is barely pink and the next is deep salmon. What usually separates them?
options: The deeper one is the sweeter wine
The deeper one sat on the skins for a few hours longer
The deeper one had red wine blended into it
The deeper one was picked riper and later
cards.a: Skin time, in hours. Press red grapes at once and the juice runs almost colourless; a few hours on the skins darkens it. Colour tells you nothing about sweetness. Blending red into white is barred for still rosé in the EU and allowed for sparkling, which is how pink Champagne is made.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Barolo and Barbaresco are the same grape grown a few miles apart. Why does Barbaresco drink well younger?
options: Barbaresco may soften the blend with a second grape
Barbaresco is picked early, so its tannins never fully form
Barbaresco is fermented on the skins for a shorter time by law
It sits lower and warmer, ripens sooner, and is asked to age less
cards.a: Both are Nebbiolo and neither may hold anything else. Barbaresco lies lower, nearer the Tanaro river and warmer, so its tannin ripens earlier. The rules follow the fruit: Barolo needs 38 months of ageing with 18 in wood, Barbaresco 26 with 9.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A July Uva from Sri Lanka smells of menthol and wintergreen. Where does that come from?
options: Eucalyptus planted through the estates as windbreaks
A longer wither before the leaf is rolled
The bush is stressed by a hot dry wind and defends itself
A cooler, slower oxidation in the mountain air
cards.a: Stress. From July the kachchan wind comes down off the mountains dry and warm, leaving Uva in a rain shadow, and the leaf answers by raising methyl salicylate, the wintergreen compound. It lasts a few weeks a year. The rest of the estate's crop does not taste like it.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A twenty-year-old raw puerh and a young cake pushed hard in damp storage both pour dark. What separates them in the cup?
options: The old one is darker still, and the damp one browner
The old one has lost every trace of bitterness
Only the dry leaf tells you, since both taste much alike
The old one still grips and sweetens; the damp one smells of cellar
cards.a: Age softens a tea without emptying it. A well-kept old cake still has grip and a sweetness that returns after you swallow, with camphor, dried plum and old wood behind it. Damp storage buys the colour in a couple of years and leaves a musty note that never brews out.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why is almost all modern tea planted from cuttings rather than grown from seed?
cards.a: The plant will not fertilise itself, so every seed is a cross and every seedling comes out different. A cutting is a clone, so a field ripens and tastes alike, and a cultivar name, which is just that clone's name, means something. Old seed-grown gardens are uneven, and valued for it.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A green tea that tasted clean in the shop is sour and hay-like a month later. What most likely went wrong?
options: It was picked too late, at the coarse end of the season
It was roasted too hard in the last firing of the batch
It was stored too cold, and the cold has flattened it
It was never dried far enough, so the leaf kept reacting
cards.a: The last drying is what makes tea shelf-stable. It takes the leaf to roughly 2–3% moisture and shuts the chemistry down. Left wetter than that, the leaf keeps oxidising inside the packet and can grow mould. Green tea shows it first, because nothing in it was meant to change.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Tea and coffee both deliver caffeine. Why does tea's tend to feel steadier?
options: Theanine, an amino acid coffee does not carry, comes with it
Tea's caffeine is a chemically different molecule from coffee's
Hot water extracts a gentler form of the molecule
Tea's tannins destroy part of the caffeine as it brews
cards.a: Theanine, the amino acid behind tea's brothy sweetness, arrives in the same cup. Trials pairing the two do show steadier attention, though they dose far more theanine than a cup holds. Tea also simply carries less caffeine per cup, which is part of the answer.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Taiwanese competition tea is judged from one fixed brew. What does that do to the winning style?
options: It favours whichever tea was picked closest to judging day
It favours a tea that survives a punishing over-brew
It favours the darkest and most heavily roasted lots
It favours the highest-grown tea in the field
cards.a: Three grams sit in 150ml of boiling water for six minutes, blind, with taste and aroma carrying most of the score. Six minutes is far longer than anyone drinks, so any harshness is dragged into the cup. A winner is a tea with nothing to hide, which is not the same as the best one to drink.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Most Champagne carries no vintage year. What is the blender actually doing?
cards.a: Erasing the harvest. A house holds back reserve wines from earlier years and blends them into the new base, so the non-vintage bottle tastes the same whenever you buy it. That consistency is the house style, and it is the product. A vintage is declared only when one year can stand alone.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A young tannic red and a forty-year-old one both get decanted. Same reason?
options: Yes: both are being separated from the sediment they threw
Yes: both need air before they will open up in the glass
No: the old one is poured off its sediment, and air flattens it
No: the young one is mainly being warmed by the pouring
cards.a: Two different jobs. A young wine is decanted for oxygen, which lifts the aroma and takes the edge off the tannin. An old one is decanted only to leave its sediment behind. The aromas decades built can fade within the hour, so pour gently and drink it soon.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Tempranillo takes its name from ripening early. What does that cost the grower?
cards.a: Acidity. It reaches sugar and colour fast and drops acid on the way, so on a warm site the wine finishes soft and short. Rioja answers with altitude and cool nights, and with blending partners: Garnacha for body, Graciano and Mazuelo for the acid and lift Tempranillo runs out of.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Brunello di Montalcino and Chianti Classico are both Sangiovese. Why may Brunello use nothing else?
options: Montalcino is warmer and drier, so the grape ripens fully on its own
Brunello ages so long that any blending partner would fade out of it
Chianti Classico is required to include a share of white grapes
Montalcino sits higher, so its fruit holds more acidity
cards.a: Warmth. Montalcino lies south of Chianti Classico, warmer and drier, and Sangiovese ripens there fully enough to carry a wine by itself: Brunello must be 100% of it. Chianti Classico is cooler, keeps a sharper red-fruited bite, and may fill out with up to 20% of other red grapes.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Tasting notes sort aromas into primary, secondary and tertiary. What is that sorting?
cards.a: Where the smell came from. Primary is the grape and the site: fruit, flower, herb, pepper. Secondary is the making: yeast and bread, butter, vanilla and toast off the oak. Tertiary is time: nut, dried fruit, mushroom, leather. Placing a smell tells you what the wine has been through.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A heavily roasted oolong tastes harsh and ashy the week it is made. What fixes it?
options: Months of resting, which lets the fire settle back
A hotter brew, which drives the smoke off
A second, lighter roast laid over the first
Nothing, since the roast was taken too far
cards.a: Time in the jar. Charcoal-roasted oolong is rested for weeks or months, tui huo, letting the fire retreat: moisture redistributes through the leaf and the char note sinks back under the tea. A heavy roast can want a year. Buying one straight off the fire is buying it early.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Lapsang Souchong is smoked over pine. When in the making does the smoke go in?
options: A pine oil is brushed onto the finished leaf
The dry tea is stored with pine chips until it takes the scent
The smoke rises through the rooms where the leaf withers and dries
The leaf is fired in a wok over pine instead of charcoal
cards.a: It is built in, not added on. At Tongmu, in the Wuyi hills of northern Fujian, the leaf sits in a wooden smokehouse over a pine fire. It takes smoke while it withers, and again while it dries. The campfire version is an export style; the local one is faintly smoky.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A fine foam rises on the first infusion. Is something wrong with the tea?
cards.a: No. The leaf carries saponins, natural foaming compounds that lower the water's surface tension, and a fast pour whips them up. Bud-heavy and freshly made teas throw the most of it. The old habit is to skim it off with the lid, but there is nothing in it to avoid.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why does a supermarket black tea taste the same in June as it did in January?
cards.a: Because it is built to. A blender tastes samples from many gardens and mixes to a fixed specification, then rewrites the recipe as the crops change so that the cup does not. A single-garden tea is the opposite bargain: it moves with the season, and that movement is what you bought.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A cheap young white smells loudly of pear drop and banana. Where was that aroma made?
options: In the grape skins, and picking earlier keeps more of it
In the ferment, run cold so the yeast makes more esters
In the sugar left behind when the ferment was stopped
In the oak, from a light toast that reads as sweet fruit
cards.a: Yeast builds acetate esters, and a cold ferment near 12–16C keeps far more of them in the wine. Isoamyl acetate is the pear drop and banana one. Those esters slowly come apart in bottle, so the smell is loudest in the first year and thin by the third.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A bottle of Vouvray, a Loire Chenin Blanc, says nothing at all about sweetness. What could be inside?
options: Dry wine only, since sweet Vouvray must be labelled moelleux
Off-dry, the one still style the appellation permits
Anything from bone dry to sweet, since the word is optional
Sparkling, since the still wines must always state sweetness
cards.a: One appellation covers the whole scale: sec for dry, demi-sec for off-dry, moelleux for sweet. Printing the word is voluntary for still Vouvray and plenty of growers leave it off. Low alcohol is the usual hint that fermentation was stopped with sugar still in.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A list offers Gevrey-Chambertin, and Chambertin at ten times the price. Same place?
options: Yes, Chambertin is the trade short form of the village name
No, Chambertin is a grand cru and the village took its name
No, Chambertin is the older name and the village replaced it
Yes, but Chambertin must come from vines of a certain age
cards.a: In 1847 the village of Gevrey annexed the name of its greatest vineyard, and others down the Côte d'Or followed, as far as the two Montrachets. A grand cru is its own appellation and stands alone on the label, so the bare vineyard name outranks the hyphenated village every time.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Southern Rhône vines are often grown as low free-standing bushes with no wires. Why?
cards.a: The mistral, a cold dry wind that funnels down the valley and can gust past 90km/h. A gobelet bush sits low, takes the wind without shredding and shades its own fruit. That same wind dries the canopy after rain, which is why so much of the region farms organically.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot ripen in one vineyard. What makes the Merlot softer?
options: Merlot is picked earlier, before much tannin has formed
Merlot's tannin is a softer molecule that binds less saliva
Merlot carries more sugar, and alcohol covers the tannin
Merlot's berries are larger and thinner-skinned
cards.a: Colour and tannin sit in the skin and the juice sits in the pulp, so the ratio between them decides extraction before a winemaker touches anything. Cabernet's small thick-skinned berries give far more skin per litre. It is also why rain before harvest thins a wine.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Two red Châteauneuf-du-Pape wines, from the southern Rhône, taste nothing alike. How much does the appellation fix?
options: Grenache must lead, at a minimum of half the blend
Each estate registers a recipe and must then hold to it
The blend is free, but white grapes are barred from the red
Very little: it names the permitted varieties and no proportions
cards.a: It permits thirteen varieties by name, or eighteen if the white, grey and black versions of some of them are counted apart, and then sets no percentages. White grapes may go into the red. So one bottle is nearly pure Grenache and its neighbour a field blend.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why is a low yield not on its own a promise of ripe fruit?
options: Ripeness is set by the leaves feeding the crop, not by tonnage
Low yields raise sugar and drop acid at exactly the same rate
Thinning after the fruit colours can no longer change anything
Rootstock rather than crop size decides how fast a vine ripens
cards.a: Ripening is a supply problem: the leaves make the sugar and the crop spends it. Growers reckon on roughly a square metre of healthy leaf for every kilo of fruit. A cramped, shaded vine carrying a tiny crop can still fall short of ripeness.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Viognier is picked riper than almost any other white grape. What forces that?
options: Its thick skins need heat before their tannin softens
Its acidity climbs late, so an early pick tastes flabby
Its apricot and blossom aroma arrives only at the very end
Its sugar builds so slowly that harvest cannot come sooner
cards.a: The perfume that makes the grape worth growing builds in the last days on the vine, and a Viognier picked before it smells of very little. Waiting costs acidity and adds alcohol, which is why Condrieu, its home in the northern Rhône, is full, oily and soft.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: In Rías Baixas on Spain's wet Atlantic coast, Albariño is trained on pergolas overhead. Why?
cards.a: Rain, well over 1300mm of it a year. A canopy lifted head high on stone pergolas lets wind through to dry the bunches and keeps them off the damp ground, because rot is the region's central problem. Albariño's unusually thick skins are part of the same answer.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: In the vineyards of Austria's Wachau, Riesling takes the stone terraces and Grüner Veltliner the ground below. Why?
cards.a: Water. The terraces are bare primary rock, gneiss and granite, holding almost none, and Riesling handles that stress and takes its edge from it. Grüner Veltliner, Austria's own white grape, is thirstier, so it sits on the loess below: wind-blown silt that holds moisture.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Japanese green tea leaves the farm as aracha, crude leaf still full of stem and dust. What does a refiner do to it?
options: Steams it a second time, which sets the needle shape
Blends it with other gardens, and nothing more
Gives it hi-ire, a final firing that settles the aroma
Allows a light oxidation to take off the grassy edge
cards.a: A refining house sorts out the stem and dust, then fires the leaf again: hi-ire, the finishing fire. How hard it fires is a house decision, so one field can reach you smelling of toasted nuts or of cut grass. Shincha is deliberately fired lightest.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why does matcha go stale in weeks when leaf tea keeps for a year?
options: Grinding heats the leaf and starts oxidation before you buy it
Shading leaves it full of fats and pigments that break down fast
The powder pulls water out of the air far faster than leaf can
Milling multiplies the surface meeting the air enormously
cards.a: Every particle is a freshly cut face. Milled to a few microns, the leaf meets far more oxygen and light than a rolled needle does. The vivid green dulls toward khaki and the sweetness gives way to hay. Buy small tins, and keep them cold and sealed.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Usucha, thin tea, and koicha, thick tea, come from the same tin of matcha. What actually changes?
options: The water temperature, which is much lower for the thick one
The dose and the water, so the thick one is kneaded rather than whisked
The whisk, which needs far more tines for the thicker style
The grind, which is coarser for the thick one to hold back bitterness
cards.a: Roughly 2g of powder whisked into 70ml gives usucha, foamed and light. Koicha is about double the powder in half the water, stirred slowly to a smooth paste rather than beaten. Nothing bitter survives that concentration, so koicha uses only top grades.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: GABA tea is neither a plant nor a place. What is done to the leaf?
options: It is aged under pressure until microbes build the compound
It is picked after dark, when the leaf holds the most of it
It comes from a bred cultivar that carries the compound already
It is sealed under nitrogen, with the oxygen shut out, for hours
cards.a: With no air to work with, the leaf turns anaerobic and converts its glutamic acid into GABA, a nerve signalling compound the body also makes itself. A Japanese researcher, Tsushida, found the trick in 1987. Taiwan makes most of it now, and it carries a sour, stewed-fruit note.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Anji Bai Cha, from Anji county in Zhejiang, translates as Anji white tea, yet it is a green tea. Why the name?
cards.a: The leaf, not the class. Its Bai Ye No.1 bush turns albino in a narrow band around 20C. Early spring shoots come out pale jade with green veins, and stack amino acids where polyphenols would normally go. Warmer or colder it greens over, so the picking window is short.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A shop offers you a dark tea called Liu Bao. What are you being sold?
options: Guangxi's own dark tea, basket aged and known for betel nut
A grade of shou puerh, taken from the sixth pick of the year
Leaf from six mountains, blended and pressed into one brick
A Fujian white tea gone dark and sweet in very long storage
cards.a: Liu Bao comes from Wuzhou in Guangxi, not Yunnan. It is wet piled to ferment, then aged for years in huge breathing bamboo baskets. Cultivar, that pile and the long ageing together build binglang xiang, betel nut fragrance: cooling, medicinal, faintly sweet.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Where does the creamy smell in a Taiwanese milk oolong come from?
options: Steaming the leaf over milk during the final drying
A very light oxidation, which leaves lactic notes behind
The Jin Xuan cultivar, which builds those compounds itself
High mountain cloud, which slows the leaf and sweetens it
cards.a: Jin Xuan was bred in Taiwan in 1981 and carries lactones that read as cream, so lightly oxidised it comes out milky on its own. Much of what is exported as milk oolong is that cultivar sprayed with flavouring, which is louder and holds through every steep.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Two Wuyi rock oolongs from northern Fujian, roasted alike: Rou Gui, named for cassia bark, and Shui Xian, an old large-leaf bush. Which tastes how?
options: Rou Gui is loud and spicy, Shui Xian broad and mellow
Rou Gui is the smooth honeyed one, Shui Xian the sharper one
Rou Gui comes off older bushes, so it gives the thicker soup
They are one leaf under two names, for two levels of roast
cards.a: Cultivar, showing through one process. Rou Gui is named for cassia bark and pushes a cinnamon-sweet aroma out front. Shui Xian is an old large-leaf cultivar giving a thicker, honeyed, woodier cup. The Wuyi saying: none more aromatic, none more mellow.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: How does a loose oolong leaf end up as a hard little ball?
cards.a: Warm leaf is packed into a cloth bag, twisted into a ball and pressed under a machine. Then it is tipped out, broken up and reheated, and the cycle runs again. It repeats for hours. Empty a spent pot and the leaves unfold whole. The step is cloth rolling, tuan rou.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why do tasters smell the dry leaf, then the wet leaf, then the liquor separately?
cards.a: Because the aromatics leave in order of how volatile they are, which roughly tracks their weight. The lightest come off the hot wet leaf in the first seconds, which is why the lid goes straight under the nose. Heavier ones stay dissolved in the cup.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Cahors in south west France is Malbec's original home. How does its wine differ from an Argentine Malbec?
options: Lighter and fruitier, since Malbec is only a minor part there
Much the same: a grape's character travels wherever it is planted
Paler, because a cooler site pulls less colour out of the skins
Firmer, darker and more savoury, off a cooler and damper site
cards.a: Cahors is cooler and much damper, so tannin ripens slowly and the wine finishes firm and savoury rather than plush. Medieval buyers called it the black wine. The appellation must be at least 70% Malbec, with only Merlot and Tannat beside it.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One Wachau bottle says Federspiel and the next says Smaragd. What is that ladder measuring?
options: How long the wine was aged before release
Residual sugar, running from dry through to sweet
The alcohol the wine finished at, all three tiers being dry
The vineyard's rank, from ordinary land up to the best sites
cards.a: Ripeness at harvest, expressed as finished alcohol, because every tier is dry. Steinfeder stops at 11.5%, Federspiel runs 11.5–12.5%, Smaragd starts at 12.5%. The word on the label promises weight and says nothing about sweetness.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Wherever the tea bush sees a real winter, the spring picking costs the most. What is the plant doing that earns that?
options: Storing sugars and amino acids all winter, which the first shoots then spend
Concentrating its sap, because cold slows how much water the roots take up
Growing younger, smaller leaves, and young leaf is always sweeter than old
Answering frost damage by raising its aromatic compounds, as a wound response
cards.a: Cold stops growth, and through the dormant months the bush banks sugars and amino acids in its roots and wood. The first flush is grown out of that store rather than out of the day's sunlight, so it comes up sweet and low in bitterness.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Green tea and light oolong keep for a year or more in a freezer. What ruins them on the way out?
options: Light reaching the leaf every time the freezer door is opened
Ice crystals rupturing the leaf cells and releasing the enzymes inside
Condensation, if the pack is opened before it has warmed to room temperature
Dry freezer air pulling out the last of the leaf's moisture
cards.a: Cold slows the oxidation that dulls green leaf, and Japan and Taiwan freeze stock as a matter of course. The danger is on the way out: a cold pack opened in a warm kitchen pulls water straight onto bone-dry leaf. Let it reach room temperature before the seal is broken.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A red smells of farmyard and sticking plaster, and the same case gets louder year on year. What is at work?
options: Cork taint, which is why it varies from bottle to bottle within a case
Brettanomyces, a yeast that lives in barrel wood and keeps working in the bottle
Oxidation, as the cork slowly admits more air than it should
Reduction, which a hard swirl in the glass will drive off
cards.a: Brettanomyces needs only traces of sugar and hides in the pores of old oak. It turns acids the wine already holds into compounds that smell of horse, leather and plaster, and being alive it carries on in bottle. Low acidity and light sulphur let it in.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Saint-Émilion reclassifies its châteaux roughly every ten years. What follows from a rank that can be lost?
options: In practice nothing, because no estate has ever been demoted
Estates rise and fall on it, and the greatest names can refuse to enter
The rank belongs to the vineyard land, so it survives any owner
Every vintage must be submitted, or the rank lapses automatically
cards.a: The rank has to be re-earned on a dossier of tastings, terroir and reputation, so it can go down as well as up. Cheval Blanc, Ausone and Angélus withdrew across 2021 and 2022 rather than be judged, leaving Pavie and the newly promoted Figeac alone at the top.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A Muscadet label says sur lie. What does that phrase bind the producer to?
cards.a: The wine stays on its fermentation lees through the winter, then goes into bottle straight off them, never racked. That keeps the dissolved carbon dioxide you feel as a faint prickle. Sur lie is simply on the lees. Muscadet is the place, Melon de Bourgogne the grape.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A Wuyi rock oolong, from the cliffs of northern Fujian, is offered as zhengyan, banyan or zhoucha. What do those name?
options: Three grades of leaf, from bud-heavy down to coarse and stemmy
Three ages of bush, from young plantings up to old trees
Three positions on the map, from the cliff ravines out to the riverbanks
Three roasting levels, from light firing through to heavy charcoal
cards.a: Three positions, from the cliff outward. The core ravines are zhengyan, true rock. The lower ground around them is banyan, half rock. Along the streams sits zhoucha, sandbank tea, on soil deep and rich enough that the bush grows fast and the cup comes out thinner.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A bag from Muzha in Taipei is labelled tieguanyin. What might that word be describing?
options: The village it came from, as with most Chinese tea names
The cultivar alone, since the name belongs to that one bush
The roast, which in Muzha is always long and heavy charcoal
The bush or the method: other cultivars made that way take the name
cards.a: It names a cultivar and a way of making tea at once. Zhang Naimiao carried tieguanyin cuttings from Anxi to Muzha in 1895 and the heavy repeated charcoal roast came with them. Other bushes made that way sell under the name, so zheng cong, true bush, marks the original.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Mourvèdre is a minority partner across most of southern France but leads in Bandol. What limits it?
cards.a: It ripens very late and needs real heat to finish. Picked short it comes out hard and green with a gamey edge that never resolves, so growers plant much of it only where autumn stays warm. Bandol, on the Mediterranean coast, requires at least half of it.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Alsace names 51 grand cru vineyards. What does the title stop a grower doing on that land?
options: Irrigating, which is forbidden outright on classified sites
Bottling most grape varieties under the name, which is held to four
Selling the fruit on, since a grand cru has to be estate bottled
Blending, because every grand cru wine must come from one parcel
cards.a: Reserved for Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat, with named exceptions: Sylvaner at Zotzenberg, blends at Kaefferkopf and Altenberg de Bergheim, and red Pinot Noir on three sites since 2022. Classified rows carrying Pinot Blanc are bottled as plain Alsace.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One grower bottles the same Champagne at zero sugar and at nine grams a litre. What actually changes?
options: The alcohol rises a little as that added sugar ferments out
The zero version keeps longer, since sugar speeds oxidation
The sweeter one reads lower in acid and fuller in the mouth
Only the sweetness: nine grams sits below what most can taste
cards.a: Sugar suppresses the perception of acid and lends a little weight, so one wine reads taut and severe and the other rounder. It is why a zero dosage Champagne, bottled with no sugar added at all, needs a ripe and long-aged base: nothing is laid over its edges.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Nearly all Japanese green tea is steamed. What is done differently to kamairicha?
options: It is fired in a hot drum, so the leaf comes out curled
It is shaded for weeks before picking, as gyokuro is
It is roasted brown after drying, which is where the colour comes from
It is left to oxidise briefly before firing, which darkens it
cards.a: It is pan-fired instead of steamed. The leaf tumbles in the drum rather than passing through the rollers that straighten sencha into needles, so it comes out curled and loose. Kyushu makes nearly all of it, and that curl in the packet gives it away.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Anhua in Hunan presses dark tea into a log as tall as a man. How is that log actually built?
cards.a: Steamed leaf is packed into a woven bamboo tube lined with leaves, then squeezed down its length with poles until it is solid, near 36kg. The damp casing shrinks as it dries and keeps tightening it. The log stands outdoors in sun and dew, and reaches you sawn into discs.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A bottle says Cream Sherry, from Jerez in southern Spain. What is in the glass?
options: A wine raised in its own sweeter solera from the beginning
A blend of Fino and Oloroso, which is where the richness comes from
A wine whose fermentation was halted early to leave the sugar behind
A dry oxidative wine sweetened after ageing, usually with Pedro Ximénez
cards.a: A dry base, usually Oloroso, blended with sweet wine once it has aged. Pedro Ximénez grapes are laid out in the sun until they are half raisin, so the must is too sugary to ferment far. Sweetness in sherry is nearly always added at the end.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A Vintage Port and a Late Bottled Vintage from the same harvest stand side by side. What separates them?
options: How long each sat in wood before bottling: about two years, or four to six
The fruit, since LBV is drawn from the lesser vineyards
Sweetness, because LBV is fortified later and finishes drier
The blend, since Vintage comes from one vineyard and LBV does not
cards.a: Time in wood, and what that leaves to do afterwards. Vintage goes into bottle at about two years and matures there for decades, unfiltered, so it throws a crust and must be decanted. LBV is usually filtered on bottling, pours clear and is ready on release.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Ilam in eastern Nepal sits on the same ridges as Darjeeling and can taste remarkably like it. What is the real difference?
