options: A protected name, which Darjeeling holds and Nepal has nothing like
The processing, since Nepal makes only shredded leaf for teabags
The bushes, which in Nepal are the large-leaved Assam variety
The climate, since Nepal lies lower down and warmer
cards.a: A protected name, not a break in the geology. Darjeeling's is legally defined and closed to leaf from outside it, and Nepal has no equivalent. So very similar tea off the same ridge sells for less, and much of it leaves the country anonymously into blends.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A charcoal-roasted oolong costs several times what the same leaf roasted in an oven does. What is being paid for?
cards.a: Labour, mostly. Charcoal is a bed of embers under ash beneath a bamboo basket, radiating low heat for hours and repeated over months, and someone has to tend it. An oven holds a set temperature exactly and cheaply. Makers hold that the slow fire sinks deeper.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why does an oolong maker watch the sky more anxiously than a green tea maker?
cards.a: Oolong opens with shai qing, sun withering: the leaf is spread outdoors for a short spell to soften and start its aroma chemistry, then carried in to cool and rest before the tossing begins. Cloud or rain forces it inside under fans and the tea comes out duller.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Longjing leaf lies flat and smooth rather than curled or twisted. What made it that shape?
cards.a: The pressing. A hand holds the leaf flat against the hot wok as it fires. So three jobs happen at once: the heat kills the enzymes, the leaf dries, and the shape is set. Elsewhere those are three separate stages. It goes into the wok twice, with a rest between.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One Bordeaux label says Saint-Émilion Grand Cru and the next says Grand Cru Classé. What separates them?
options: Grand Cru is the rank and Grand Cru Classé the appellation
Grand Cru is an appellation open to all; Classé is a rank
Grand Cru names the vineyard, Grand Cru Classé the château
Both are ranks, and Classé is simply the tier above
cards.a: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is an appellation, not a prize. Any grower on the same ground may use it by cropping lower, reaching a higher minimum alcohol and ageing longer. Grand Cru Classé is the ranked list inside it, and most bottles saying Grand Cru are not on it.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A bottle from the Jura, in eastern France, holds 62cl where a standard bottle holds 75cl. What is that size recording?
options: A tax band that once applied to strong white wine
The measure fixed by the monks who first made it
What one litre has left after six years in cask
The share held back each year to top up older barrels
cards.a: Vin jaune sits in barrel six years and three months and is never topped up, under a voile: a film of yeast that shields it from the air. About 38% evaporates away, and that short bottle, the clavelin, holds what a litre became. The grape is Savagnin.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Gewurztraminer smells of rose and lychee and ripens to high sugar. Why does a warm site ruin it?
options: It holds almost no acid, so the heat leaves it flabby
Its rose and lychee perfume only forms below a set temperature
Its pink skins bake in strong sun and turn the wine bitter
Heat drives the sugar so high that the ferment sticks and stops
cards.a: It has no acid to spare. It ripens early to a lot of sugar and sheds acid on the way, so a warm site gives a broad, soft wine at 14% with nothing holding it up. Cool sites keep some bite under the perfume. Its pink skins are why it pours deep gold.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A garden stops plucking for a fortnight in the middle of the season. What is the bush doing?
options: Recovering from a pruning done earlier in the year
Flowering, which stops it putting out leaf
Resting, its growing tip closed into a blind bud
Shedding leaf ahead of the dry months
cards.a: Shoots grow in bursts rather than steadily. After a few leaves the tip sets a banjhi, a blind bud that makes no new leaf, and the shoot stalls until the stem below widens enough to feed it. Pluckers wait out that pause, and it is what puts gaps between pickings.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Turkey and Georgia grow tea further north than anywhere else. What lets the plant survive there?
options: Bushes raised from seed, which root deeper than cuttings
Small-leaf sinensis, which takes a hard winter
Grafting tea onto a hardy ornamental camellia
Big-leaf assamica, whose thick leaves resist frost
cards.a: Cold tolerance belongs to the plant. Small-leaf sinensis survives winters down to around minus 10C; big-leaf assamica, the tropical variety behind Assam and puerh, does not. That split draws the tea map, so a big broad leaf in the pot grew without a real winter.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A dry Fino sherry sold en rama, meaning raw, pours hazy and smells far louder than the standard bottling. What was left out?
options: The filtering and fining a normal bottling gets
The fortification, so it goes out at its natural strength
The years of ageing, so it is bottled while still young
The blending, so it comes from one single cask
cards.a: The filtering. Sherry is normally filtered hard to stay bright on a shelf, which strips the solids carrying its texture and the smell of flor, the yeast film it ages under. En rama is drawn in spring when the flor is thickest, and bottled almost untouched. Drink it soon.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Champagne is pressed in fractions and some houses use only the first. What is wrong with the juice that follows?
options: It is too low in sugar to reach the alcohol the method needs
It has begun oxidising in the press and browns in the wine
It is so high in acid that bottle age never softens it
It carries more colour and potassium, and ages far worse
cards.a: The first 2050 litres from a 4000kg press is the cuvée: clean, sharp and long-lived. The 500 litres of taille squeezed after carry more colour and more potassium, and potassium strips acidity out. Taille gives a fruitier wine young and a tired one at ten years.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Two unglazed Yixing pots: one a fine red clay fired almost dense, one a coarse sandy clay left porous. What changes in the cup?
options: The porous one lifts aroma; the dense one softens the tea
The dense one lifts aroma; the porous one softens the tea
Nothing you could taste: the clay only changes how the pot looks
The porous one holds far more heat, so it opens tight leaf faster
cards.a: Density. Zhu ni, a fine red ore from the Yixing hills in Jiangsu, fires almost tight, so little soaks in and a fragrant oolong comes through loud. Duan ni is coarse and far more porous, so it absorbs more and rounds bitterness off, which suits raw puerh or a heavy roast.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A jar of roasted oolong laid down for ten years gets re-roasted every year or two. What is that maintenance for?
options: To drive out moisture the leaf has taken from the air
To push the roast a shade darker with each pass
To restart oxidation that has stalled inside the jar
To kill anything living on the leaf before it is sold
cards.a: Leaf pulls water out of the air, and past a few percent it turns soft and grassy again, which sellers call fan qing, returning to green. A light re-firing drives that water back out. Aged oolong is tended, not left alone, and a heavier first roast buys longer gaps.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Banyuls and Maury, sweet reds from Roussillon on France's border with Spain, are fortified while still on their skins. What does that buy?
cards.a: Grape spirit goes into the must while it is still fermenting. Left on the skins, it keeps macerating in alcohol for days after the yeast dies, and alcohol pulls out colour and tannin that water cannot reach. The addition is mutage, the category vin doux naturel.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Yellow tea is the rarest of the six Chinese classes. What keeps producers off it?
cards.a: The sealed yellowing that makes the class adds days of warm damp handling to a crop that has to be sold fresh, and it can go wrong. The gain is subtle enough that many buyers cannot pick it from a good green. Green tea is quicker, safer and better paid.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A puerh wrapper reads 7542 and gives no other name. What are those four digits saying?
cards.a: A blending recipe. The first two digits are the year the recipe was written, 1975 here, the third the leaf grade with higher meaning coarser, the fourth the factory, all in Yunnan: 1 Kunming, 2 Menghai, 3 Xiaguan. Standardised in 1976. The year is the recipe's, not the tea's.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Silver Needle, a white tea of buds alone, looks furred and silver, and the cup fills with tiny floating hairs. What are they?
cards.a: Fine hairs the bud grows to shield itself from sun and insects. They are what make it look silver, and they come loose in hot water. So a faint haze of hairs in the cup is a sign of bud-heavy leaf, not a fault. The Chinese is bai hao, white down.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Zinfandel routinely finishes above 15% and shows a raisined edge. What in the vineyard causes both?
options: Very thin skins, so the berries shrivel on the vine in heat
Its sugar ripens well ahead of its tannin, as in any hot site
It is picked deliberately late, to build sweetness in the fruit
Berries in a single bunch ripen at wildly different times
cards.a: One bunch holds raisins next to green fruit whatever day it is picked, so the grower is always choosing which fault to take. The raisined berries carry huge sugar and the yeast turns that into alcohol. Primitivo in Puglia is the same grape under an Italian name.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Amarone and Recioto della Valpolicella both begin with grapes dried on racks for months. What separates them?
options: Recioto's ferment is halted early, so its sugar stays in
Recioto is dried for longer, so it concentrates further
Amarone is fortified with grape spirit and Recioto is not
Amarone is matured in oak and Recioto goes straight to bottle
cards.a: Where the ferment is allowed to stop. Corvina and the other grapes of Valpolicella, in the hills above Verona, lose water on the racks into winter, concentrating sugar. Run the ferment out and every gram becomes alcohol: Amarone, dry and near 16%. Halt it and you have Recioto.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Jin Jun Mei sells for more than almost any other Chinese black tea. What is actually in the tin?
options: Leaf smoked over pine, in the manner of the village's older tea
The first two leaves taken off old seed-grown trees
Bud and leaf blended to a fixed house recipe each year
Unopened buds alone, with no smoke on them at all
cards.a: Buds only, picked before they open, if it is genuine. Made at Tongmu in 2005, the Wuyi village behind pine-smoked Lapsang Souchong, as an unsmoked luxury off the same bushes. The name was never trademarked, so most tins now hold leaf as well as bud.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A tin says ceremonial grade matcha. What has that phrase been checked against?
cards.a: Nothing. No Japanese body defines it and no rule restricts it; it was coined for export buyers. Harvest, shade and mill decide the powder. Ask for first-flush leaf and stone grinding, then judge the tin: bright jade rather than khaki, and no grit between the fingers.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: One oolong tin from Anxi in Fujian is marked qing xiang and the next nong xiang. What is that pair of words sorting?
cards.a: How far the leaf was baked. Qing xiang, light aroma, is barely fired and stays green and floral. Nong xiang, dense aroma, is baked on and comes out amber, nutty and rounder. Chen xiang, aged aroma, is the third. They are national standard types, not shop language.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One Prosecco says Brut and the bottle beside it says Extra Dry. Which is the sweeter wine?
options: Extra Dry, at 12–17 grams of sugar a litre against Brut's 0–12
Brut, because Extra Dry sits one step drier on the same ladder
Brut, because Extra Dry describes the pressing and not the sugar
Neither, the two words are marketing and carry no legal limits
cards.a: The words stopped meaning what they say. The EU ladder runs Brut Nature 0–3 grams a litre, Extra Brut 0–6, Brut 0–12, then Extra Dry 12–17 and Dry 17–32. The plainer the word sounds, the sweeter the wine. Extra Dry is Prosecco's usual style.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Prosecco takes its second fermentation in a sealed pressurised tank rather than inside each bottle. What does that decide?
cards.a: Cost, and the shape of the fizz. The tank method ferments a whole batch at once in weeks, so nothing is handled bottle by bottle or locked in a cellar for years. Prosecco is also finished nearer 3 atmospheres than Champagne's 5 or 6, so its foam is softer and falls away faster.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Palomino, the sherry grape, makes a flat and neutral table wine. Why is that an advantage in Jerez?
options: It ripens late enough to hold its acidity through the Andalusian heat
Its thick skins shrug off the Atlantic damp that reaches the vineyards
Having no flavour of its own, it leaves the ageing to supply all of it
It ferments to high alcohol, so less fortifying spirit has to be added
cards.a: Everything you taste in sherry arrives after fermentation, from flor, the film of yeast a Fino ages under, or from air. A grape with a voice would be in the way. Palomino is low in acid and nearly scentless, and grows almost only on albariza, a white chalk that holds winter rain.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A tea garden is a flat hedge clipped to waist height. What is plucking itself doing to the plant?
options: Keeping the bush stressed, which is what concentrates the next shoot
Removing the growing tip, which wakes the buds below it
Thinning the canopy so light reaches the older leaves underneath
Taking the flower buds off before they can draw on the leaf
cards.a: Plucking is pruning. Apical dominance means a growing tip holds the buds below it asleep, so taking the tip wakes them and the bush answers with more shoots than it lost. That is why tea is a hedge and not the tree it would be, and why the table is cut back every few years.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Laos and Myanmar grow the same big-leaf tea and press it the same way. Why is none of it puerh?
options: Puerh has to be pressed in the year it is picked, and their cakes are not
Only leaf from old forest trees qualifies, and theirs is plantation grown
Puerh leaf is fixed hard in a pan, and theirs is dried in the sun instead
Puerh is a protected origin: Yunnan leaf, sun-dried and pressed in a listed area
cards.a: China's 2008 standard makes puerh a geographical indication, a name tied to a place: Yunnan large-leaf assamica, taken to sun-dried loose leaf and processed inside a listed set of Yunnan counties. Leaf crosses those borders constantly and is pressed anyway, so a wrapper is a claim.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Tokaji Aszu, Hungary's great sweet wine, picks the berries noble rot has shrivelled one at a time, then does not ferment them. What happens to them?
options: They are dried further on straw mats until they are almost raisins
They are pressed, and the juice is fortified with grape spirit
They are frozen, so the water can be taken out of them as ice
They are kneaded to a paste and steeped in must or young wine
cards.a: Aszú berries are mashed to a dough and steeped in must or wine of the same vintage. So the sugar is drawn out rather than fermented in, and a slow, incomplete ferment follows. A puttony was the 25kg hod. Since 2013 every Aszú must reach 120 grams of sugar a litre.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One bottle sits five years at a steady 18C, another swings from 10C to 20C every day. Which fares worse?
options: The steady one, because 18C is above the safe ceiling for long keeping
Neither, since a sound cork seals whatever the room outside it does
The swinging one: the wine expands and contracts and works air past the cork
The swinging one, because the cold half of each cycle halts the ageing
cards.a: A steady 18C only ages a wine faster than a cold cellar would. A daily swing pumps it up the neck and back, drawing air in and eventually pushing wine past the capsule. Light is the other one: blue wavelengths turn a white or a sparkling wine oniony, which is why the glass is green.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Decaffeinated tea reads thin and hollow beside the same leaf with its caffeine still in. Why?
options: Caffeine itself supplies much of what is felt as a tea's body
Decaffeinating needs a second firing, and that drives the aroma off
The leaf has to be cut small first, so it goes stale before it is sold
Nothing removes caffeine alone: flavour compounds come out with it
cards.a: Caffeine is stripped with carbon dioxide under pressure or with a solvent, and none of them can tell it from the polyphenols and aromatics beside it. Ethyl acetate is the cheap route and costs the most flavour, and naturally decaffeinated on a box means that solvent, not water.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Dian Hong, the black tea of Yunnan, is thick and malty where a Fujian black tea is fine and floral. What is behind that?
options: The plant: Yunnan's big-leaf assamica carries far more polyphenol
The oxidation is run longer in Yunnan than anywhere else in China
The leaf is sun-dried in Yunnan, as puerh is, rather than fired dry
It is picked later, once the shoot has already put out three leaves
cards.a: The plant, not the making. Yunnan grows the big-leaf assamica that also becomes puerh, far heavier in polyphenol than the small-leaf bushes of the east coast. Dian Hong is not ancient either: it was set up in 1938, when war cut China off from its eastern black tea districts.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A taster tips the brewed leaf out of the pot and spreads it on the lid. What is being read off it?
options: How much the leaf has left to give, and so how many steeps to expect
Whether the water ran hot enough, which shows as leaves still shut
The pluck and the making: hand or machine cut, and how far it oxidised
The cultivar, since each one unfurls to a leaf shape of its own
cards.a: Brewing destroys the dry leaf's evidence and exposes the rest. Spread out wet, a hand pluck shows whole leaves on a torn stalk; a machine cut shows straight severed edges and stray old leaf. Colour at the rim says how far oxidation ran, and brittleness says how hard it was fired.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A small pitcher sits between the pot and the cups, and the pot is emptied into it before a single cup is filled. What is it for?
options: It brings the tea down to drinking temperature before it is served
It catches the fine broken leaf so each cup pours bright
It holds the infusion hot so the cups can be filled slowly
It blends the pour to one strength, and empties the pot so the steep ends
cards.a: Tea leaving a pot runs weak at the start and strong at the last drops, so the pitcher blends the whole infusion to one strength. Draining the pot dry also stops the brewing, which is what lets an infusion be timed in seconds. It is the fairness cup, gong dao bei.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Tossing bruises an oolong's leaf margins, so the spent leaf shows a red rim round a green centre. Why does a modern jade tieguanyin show almost none?
options: The leaf is tossed so gently that no rim ever forms on it
Heat is applied early enough to catch the margins before they brown
The long cloth rolling that shapes the ball rubs the colour out
The dried rim is beaten off the leaf afterwards, as a step of its own
cards.a: Once heat has stopped the leaf's enzymes the batch is wrapped in cloth and beaten. The oxidised margins dried hardest, so they shatter and fall away. Anxi in southern Fujian added the step for a brisker cup, and it hides how far oxidation ran. Removing the red edge.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Large flat yellowish leaves are picked out of loose puerh leaf before it is pressed into a cake. Why are they rejected?
options: They yellowed from oxidation on the way in, and would brown the cake
They would not roll into a rope, so the sort is by shape, not by taste
They are old leaf with little left to give, so they would dilute the ageing
They were scorched in the pan, and that burnt note would carry through
cards.a: The oldest leaf on the shoot, too stiff to twist up when the batch is rolled, so it stays flat and pale and is sorted out. Pressed and sold on its own it is cheap, and being mature leaf it is sweeter and lower in caffeine, so it forgives a long steep. Yellow flakes, huang pian.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Two dry whites both hold 7 grams of acid a litre, yet one is far more fragile. What is pH measuring that the total is not?
options: How sour the wine will taste, which a total cannot show
How much of the acid is tartaric rather than malic
How much acid was added in the cellar rather than grown
How strong that acid is in solution, which is what sets stability
cards.a: Titratable acidity is how much acid is there, found by neutralising it. pH counts the hydrogen ions that acid actually released, on a backwards scale where low means sharp, and it is what sets microbial risk and colour. Sourness tracks the total; stability tracks pH.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why does a high-pH wine need a far bigger sulphur dose to be as well protected as a low-pH one?
options: Sulphur binds up faster at high pH, so less of the dose stays free
Only the uncharged molecular form works, and high pH leaves far less
Less acid means more sugar survives for spoilage microbes to live on
High-pH wines oxidise faster, so the sulphur is spent defending them
cards.a: Only a small share of a wine's free sulphur dioxide is molecular SO2, the uncharged form that stuns microbes, and pH sets that share steeply. Holding the same molecular level takes about four times the free sulphur at pH 3.6 as at the sharper pH 3.0, and the legal cap does not move.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Two young reds from one grape, one at pH 3.4 and one at pH 3.9. What is different in the glass?
options: The high-pH wine looks more purple, since pigment turns blue in acid
They look alike, because colour comes from skin time and not from acid
The low-pH wine is brighter and more crimson, and holds that longer
The low-pH wine is paler, because acid strips pigment out of the skins
cards.a: Anthocyanin, the skin pigment, only shows its red form in strongly acid conditions. The pH scale runs backwards, so 3.9 is the less acid of the two. In it more pigment shifts to colourless and blue forms, and the rim reads dull and brown. Low pH also slows browning.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A grower prunes in the cold of January. Why is that when next autumn's crop size is largely fixed?
options: Cutting a dormant vine is what holds its vigour down all season
The buds left were formed last summer and already hold their bunches
The crop is settled at flowering, so pruning only sets the vine's frame
Winter reserves in the roots set the crop, whatever is left on the wood
cards.a: The buds being counted formed the previous summer, and each already carries the bunches it will push out. Winter pruning decides how many of them stay, so the crop is set before a leaf appears. A dull, shaded summer costs the following harvest as well as its own.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Leaves are pulled from around the bunches. Why does the date it is done change what it buys?
options: Early pulling ripens the fruit sooner, and late pulling comes too late
Early pulling scorches the fruit, so growers wait for the skins to thicken
Before flowering it thins the bunch itself; later it only changes exposure
It changes nothing in the fruit, only how easily the pickers work the row
cards.a: Pull before flowering and the vine has less sugar to set fruit with. Fewer berries take, so the bunch comes out small and loose, which does more against rot than spraying can. Pull at veraison, when berries colour and soften, and the bunch is made: only its light changes.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Half the bunches are cut off and left on the ground in July. What does a green harvest actually buy?
options: Concentration in proportion to what was dropped, one for one
Evenness, and the earlier it is done the more the rest swells back
More leaves per bunch, since the vine pushes new shoots to replace them
Compliance, since appellations require it once a crop runs over the limit
cards.a: Mostly evenness: cutting away the bunches lagging behind leaves a crop that ripens together. Concentration is the part that disappoints, because berries thinned early swell to fill the space they are given. It is a late correction for a crop that pruning already set too high.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Vineyards are sprayed with water all through a spring frost night. Why does sealing a bud in ice save it?
options: The ice shell seals the bud off from the colder air around it
Freezing water gives up heat, holding the bud at about zero
The spray washes frost crystals off before they can burn the shoot
Ice scatters the dawn sun, so the bud thaws slowly instead of at once
cards.a: Water gives up heat as it freezes, and that holds the bud near zero while the air falls further. Candles warm the air instead, and wind machines pull warmer air down from above it. The spray has to run until the thaw: stop halfway and the ice takes heat back out and kills the bud.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Machine harvesting is fast and cheap. What can it not do at all?
options: Pick red grapes, since the beaters bruise skins and pull harsh colour
Pick whites, whose juice starts oxidising before it reaches the cellar
Work above a certain price, because rank is tied by law to hand work
Deliver whole bunches, or choose between one bunch and the next
cards.a: A harvester shakes fruit off the stems, so what arrives is loose berries and juice, never a bunch, and it takes everything it touches. Champagne bans it, and carbonic maceration and noble rot picking both need what it cannot give. It does work at night, in the cool.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One Burgundy says mis en bouteille au domaine and the next carries only a merchant's name in Beaune. What separates them?
options: The domaine grew the fruit; the merchant bought it, often from many growers
The merchant's bottle is a lesser vineyard inside the same village
The merchant's wine was aged longer, which is what the phrase records
The domaine bottling is one barrel and the merchant's is everything else
cards.a: Who owned the grapes. Bottled at the domaine means the estate grew the fruit and bottled it itself. A négociant buys grapes, juice or finished wine and sells under its own name, so one appellation can be assembled from many growers. A cooperative is a shared cellar its members supply.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Champagne labels usually carry two small letters, NM or RM or CM. What are they recording?
options: How long the bottle lay on its lees before the yeast was removed
The sweetness of the dosage, from the driest upward
Who grew the grapes, and who made the wine
The rank of the village the fruit came from
cards.a: Who grew the fruit and who made the wine. NM, négociant manipulant, buys grapes, and nearly every famous house is one. RM, récoltant manipulant, is a grower making wine from its own vines. CM is a cooperative selling its members' wine, and MA is a buyer's own brand made by someone unnamed.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A fine dry Riesling turns thin and sour beside a fruit tart. What has the sugar in the dish done to it?
options: Pushed its acidity and bitterness forward and taken its fruit away
Coated the tongue, so the wine's aroma no longer reaches the nose
Raised the burn of the alcohol, so the wine reads hot and short
Nothing to the wine: the tart's own acidity is what you are tasting
cards.a: Sweetness on the plate raises the acidity and bitterness you read in the glass, and strips out the wine's own sweetness and fruit. So a dry wine goes hollow and sharp. The working rule: the wine has to be at least as sweet as the dish, or it loses.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Crush a fresh tea leaf and it smells of cut grass within seconds. What has just been made?
options: Green leaf volatiles, built on the spot by enzymes reaching broken fats
Chlorophyll, released from the cells and volatile once it is free
Catechins, whose bitterness the nose reads as a green smell
Theanine, sweet in the mouth and grassy in the air
cards.a: Damage lets an enzyme reach the leaf's own fats and cut them into hexenal and hexenol within seconds. Those green leaf volatiles are the smell of any cut plant, not of tea. A long wither lets most of them disperse and convert, which is why under-withered tea reads raw and grassy.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A good jasmine tea carries a heavy, almost animal weight under the flowers. What is that?
options: Smoke picked up from the baskets the leaf was dried over
Nitrogen from the blossom breaking down against the leaf
Musk, added as a fixative to hold the flower scent on the leaf
Indole, a jasmine volatile that is faecal neat and floral in traces
cards.a: Indole, one of jasmine's own compounds. On its own it smells faecal; in traces it gives the heady depth beneath the flowers. Tea flavoured with jasmine oil tends to carry the sweet top note and none of that weight, so it comes across clean, loud and thin.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A tea is roasted and comes out smelling of nuts, cocoa and toast. Where did those smells come from?
options: Sugars caramelising, which accounts for the whole of a roast aroma
Pyrazines, built by the heat out of the leaf's amino acids and sugars
Smoke drawn out of the charcoal and into the leaf
Oxidation, run all the way to its end by the heat of the roaster
cards.a: Pyrazines, a family of nitrogen compounds that heat builds out of the leaf's own amino acids and sugars. They are made rather than uncovered, which is why roasting smells of nuts and cocoa whatever went in, and why a heavy fire can bury a plain leaf.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Keemun is Anhui's famous black tea, from a district that had made only green tea for centuries. Where did it come from?
options: It was made deliberately in the 1870s, copying Fujian black tea for export
It is an old tribute tea the court had kept out of general trade
British planters set it up once Assam seed reached the province
A batch of green tea oxidised in transit and sold better that way
cards.a: It was made on purpose, for export. A Qimen man learned black tea making in Fujian and brought it home in the 1870s, because Europe wanted black tea and the district's green was not selling. Which man is disputed. Its cultivar is heavy in geraniol, so the cup reads rose-like.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Biluochun is a tiny spiral green tea from the hills above Lake Tai, west of Suzhou in Jiangsu. Why are its bushes planted in among fruit trees?
options: The trees shade the bushes, raising theanine as a cover does in Japan
Fallen fruit feeds the soil, and that is what makes the leaf so downy
Tradition holds the leaf takes up the blossom's scent as it grows
The trees break the lake wind, which would otherwise scorch the shoots
cards.a: For the blossom, by tradition. Apricot, plum, peach and loquat stand among the tea on the lake's Dongting hills, and the local account is that the leaf takes their scent up as it grows. Picked tiny and thick with down, it scorches, so brew it under 80C.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Taiping Houkui is a flat green tea with unusually long leaves, each marked with a faint criss-cross grid. What made that grid?
options: The leaf is pressed flat under a mesh-covered roller as it is shaped
The veins of the cultivar, which grows a squared-off leaf naturally
The bamboo trays it dries on, printing themselves into the wet leaf
A stamp certifying the grade before the tea may leave the county
cards.a: The leaf is laid out straight and rolled flat under a gauze mesh, which prints itself on. The flattening, with the local large-leaf bush, gives an orchid scent and very little astringency for leaves that mature. The leaves are long enough to brew upright in a tall glass.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Lu'an Guapian is finished by swinging baskets of leaf over an open charcoal fire, dozens of passes in relays. What does that buy?
options: A smoky note, built in the way pine smoke is built into Lapsang Souchong
A slow oxidation, which is what curls the leaf into its seed shape
Fierce heat in flashes, drying the leaf hard without letting it scorch
Sterilising, so the tea will keep for a year without going stale
cards.a: The basket crosses the blaze for a second at a time, so the leaf takes hard heat in flashes and never sits in it. That drives out the last water and lays a toasted sweetness on. The move is called pulling the old fire. It is the one famous Chinese green with no bud in it.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Leaving a tea bag in longer makes the cup bitter rather than stronger. What is different about loose leaf?
options: Loose leaf is younger, so it holds less tannin to give up
Loose leaf is uncompressed, so water never reaches its centre
The paper of the bag gives up a bitterness of its own once soaked
A bag holds dust and fannings, and they give up everything in a minute
cards.a: A bag holds fannings and dust, the finest fractions sorted out of production, and their surface is so large that almost everything soluble is out inside a minute. After that only astringency climbs. Whole leaf gives up its parts in order, so time is still a lever there.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A producer says the wine expresses its terroir. What is that word actually claiming?
options: The soil the vines are planted in
The appellation the wine is entitled to use
The whole natural site, and the practice that grew up to suit it
The estate's house style, held steady across vintages
cards.a: Terroir gathers the whole of a site: soil and subsoil, slope, aspect and its own local climate, and in French usage the practice that grew up to suit them. The claim it makes is narrow and testable, that a site marks its wine across vintages and across owners.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A rosé label says the wine was made by saignée. What was it a by-product of?
options: A red wine the maker wanted more concentrated
A white wine pressed off its skins after a few hours
A finished white with a little red blended into it
A second pressing of skins already used for a red
cards.a: Juice is run off a red ferment in its first hours, so what stays behind holds more skin per litre and finishes darker and firmer. The pink juice drawn away ferments on its own, and is usually weightier than a rosé from fruit picked for pink. Saignée means bleeding.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A back label says the wine had eighteen months of élevage. What was happening in that time?
options: A long, cool fermentation, run slowly on purpose
Raising in the cellar, after fermenting and before bottling
Resting in bottle before the wine was released for sale
Blending across several vintages, as a house does
cards.a: Everything between the last of the fermentation and the bottling: which vessel, how long, how much air reaches the wine, when it is blended. Most of a wine's texture is settled in that stretch, so two lots off one ferment can arrive quite different. Élevage means raising.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One Italian label says Classico and the next says Superiore. What is each word promising?
options: Both name the old heart of the zone
Both are ageing terms, like Riserva
Classico is a rule about the wine, Superiore a place
Classico is a place, Superiore a rule about the wine
cards.a: Classico is geography: the historic core of a zone, kept as a name when the boundary was widened around it. Superiore is a specification, usually a higher minimum alcohol and a lower yield, sometimes a little ageing. One says where, the other says how ripe the fruit came in.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Two German Rieslings, one labelled Trocken and one Feinherb. What separates those two words?
options: Trocken is a legal sugar limit; Feinherb has none
Feinherb is the drier of the two
Both are legal sugar limits, Feinherb the higher
Trocken describes the wine, Feinherb the vineyard
cards.a: Trocken is bound by law: broadly 4 grams of sugar a litre, stretching to 9 where acidity nearly matches the sugar. That is why a dry Riesling can taste rounder than the word suggests. Halbtrocken runs to about 12. Feinherb means nothing legally and sits loosely off-dry.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A Mosel label reads Piesporter Michelsberg and another reads Piesporter Goldtröpfchen. Are both single vineyards?
options: Yes, they are neighbouring plots in the same village
Michelsberg is a collective name spread over several villages
Goldtröpfchen is the collective one of the two
One names a vineyard and the other a producer
cards.a: Germany writes a single vineyard, an Einzellage, as village plus site. A Grosslage, one name covering a large group of vineyards, is written in exactly the same shape. Michelsberg is one of those, so the form of the name cannot tell you which you are holding.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: An old vineyard is described as a field blend. What does that fix about the wine?
options: It is blended from several vineyards rather than from one
The varieties ferment apart and are blended before bottling
The varieties are picked and fermented together, ripe or not
It is planted to one variety in several different clones
cards.a: The varieties are interplanted, so they come off on one day whether each is ready or not and go into one ferment. Nothing can be adjusted afterwards. It began as insurance rather than art: a year that ruined one variety usually spared another growing beside it.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A back label says the wine is unfined and unfiltered. What two things were skipped?
options: Any addition of sulphur, and any addition of acid
The racking that leaves sediment behind, and the topping up of the barrel
The chilling that drops out tartrate crystals, and the final blending
Clarifying with an agent that settles out, and straining through a filter
cards.a: Fining adds something that binds a target and sinks with it: clay for the proteins that haze a white, egg white for hard tannin in a red. Filtration strains instead. Both take a little texture and aroma too, so leaving them out buys weight and costs clarity and stability.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Barolo from La Morra drinks earlier than Barolo from Serralunga d'Alba. What is behind that?
options: La Morra sits lower and warmer, so its tannin ripens first
A geological line runs through the zone, and the rock differs across it
La Morra uses small new barrels and Serralunga large old casks
La Morra lies outside the historic core, so its rules are looser
cards.a: The zone straddles two geological eras. The western communes, La Morra and Barolo among them, sit on younger bluish marl heavy in clay, which gives perfume and a softer frame. Serralunga and Monforte sit on older, sandier, iron-tinged rock that gives firmer tannin and a longer wait.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A shelf holds Chianti beside Chianti Classico. What is the relationship between those two names?
options: Classico is a quality tier awarded inside the Chianti zone
Classico is the same wine given a longer ageing
They are separate appellations, and Classico is the older and smaller one
Classico marks the wines made only from a producer's own fruit
cards.a: Chianti Classico is the historic zone between Florence and Siena. In 1932 the Chianti name was stretched over a far larger area around it and the old core kept the word Classico. The two became separate appellations in 1996, and Classico crops lower and holds more Sangiovese.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Rioja Alavesa and Rioja Oriental lie at opposite ends of one region. What separates them?
options: Which weather reaches them: Atlantic at one end, Mediterranean at the other
Alavesa may plant only Tempranillo and Oriental only Garnacha
Alavesa is in the Basque country, so it is a separate appellation
Oriental sits higher and cooler, which is why it ripens later
cards.a: Rioja runs about 100km along the Ebro and climbs to the west. Alta and Alavesa sit high at the cool end, sheltered from Atlantic rain by the Sierra de Cantabria, and give the firmer, finer wines. Oriental, lower and hotter, is Mediterranean, and Garnacha ripens there to real weight.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Tempranillo makes a blacker, harder wine in Ribera del Duero than it does in Rioja. What is doing that?
options: Ribera hangs its fruit weeks longer, well into November
Ribera must use new oak where Rioja leaves it to the maker
Ribera grows a different grape that only resembles Tempranillo
Ribera sits far higher, and its local strain has smaller berries
cards.a: Ribera vineyards run from roughly 750m to 1000m on the Castilian plateau, so days are hot, nights near freezing and the season short and frost-bitten. Berries stay small, and the local strain of the grape, Tinto Fino, is smaller-berried again. More skin, less juice, darker wine.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A Burgundy label reads Meursault, with a second name under it in smaller type. What is that second name?
options: A lieu-dit, the plot's own name on the map, carrying no rank
A premier cru vineyard lying inside the village boundary
The domaine's own brand name for this particular bottling
The grand cru that the village took its own name from
cards.a: A lieu-dit is simply what a parcel is called on the map. A village wine may print it, but the law holds those letters to half the height of the appellation name so it cannot pass for a cru. Plenty are excellent sites. The name promises the place and nothing above it.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Good Huangshan Maofeng shows a small pale leaf at the foot of each bud. What is it?
options: A leaf that scorched against the wok
The fish leaf, the first small leaf a shoot opens with
A leaf from a different bush, blended in for colour
Yellowing left behind by a spell of damp storage
cards.a: Every shoot opens with a fish leaf: a small rounded one that never grows on. A bud still carrying it was taken at the very start of the flush, so graders leave it in rather than sort it out. It is why the tea is pale, downy and orchid-scented rather than grassy.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Almost every famous tea region is a hillside, yet Assam is a hot river plain barely above sea level. Why does that work?
options: The gardens are shaded, which stands in for altitude
The leaf is picked so young that the heat never reaches it
Monsoon cloud cools the plain to hill temperatures
The plant growing there is a different variety, native to that heat
cards.a: Assam is where tea's other variety grows wild. Large-leaf assamica was found in its forests in the 1820s, and until then Britain believed tea grew only in China. It wants monsoon heat and flood-plain damp, so altitude, the usual mark of fine tea, means nothing on an Assam pack.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Darjeeling tastes nothing like the tea grown on the plains below it. What is planted on those slopes?
options: A hybrid bred in Darjeeling in the twentieth century
Assam bushes that the cold has stunted into a finer leaf
The small-leaf China plant, brought up as seed in the 1840s
Wild forest tea that was never planted at all
cards.a: Darjeeling was planted from Chinese seed while the plains were planted with the large-leaf Assam variety. The small-leaf plant grows slowly between 600m and 2000m and crops very little, which is much of why Darjeeling costs what it does and reads floral rather than heavy.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Dimbula in Sri Lanka makes its best tea in January and February. What is happening then?
options: The bushes are dormant, so the first shoots come up sweetest
It is the coolest month, and cold alone makes the season
The gardens were pruned in December and are regrowing hard
The monsoon has swung round, and Dimbula has gone dry and windy
cards.a: Sri Lanka takes two monsoons from opposite directions, so one flank of the central hills is soaked while the other has gone dry and windy. Dimbula faces west and peaks in January; the eastern slopes peak in July. A date on a Ceylon pack means little until you know which flank grew it.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A broker calls a black tea brisk. What is being described?
options: A lively astringency that makes the cup refreshing
A liquor that brews out in under two minutes
A caffeine level high enough to feel
A deep, dark colour in the cup
cards.a: Brisk is a texture word, not a strength or a colour one: the clean lively grip that makes a cup refreshing and lets it carry milk. Its opposites in the trade are flat and soft. Beside it sit body, for weight in the mouth, and bright, for a clear live colour rather than a dull one.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Iced tea blends are built on Nilgiri from southern India. What is that leaf chosen for?
options: It brews at a lower temperature than other black teas
Its liquor stays clear as it cools instead of hazing over
It holds its aroma longest once sugar is added
It grows high enough to escape the monsoon entirely
cards.a: Creaming down. As black tea cools, its caffeine and tannin lock together and drop out, which clouds the cup. The stronger the liquor, the more of it. It is not a fault. Nilgiri, from the hills of Tamil Nadu, brews light, creams little, and pours clear over ice.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A Valpolicella label, from the hills above Verona, says Ripasso. What was the wine passed back over?
options: Grapes left shrivelling on racks through the winter
The skins drained from a finished Amarone fermentation
The lees of a white wine made in the same cellar
Toasted oak staves hung in the tank for a month
cards.a: The skins of a finished Amarone. Young Valpolicella is run onto them, and the sugar still in them restarts a short fermentation. The wine gains roughly a degree of alcohol, colour, tannin and a dried-fruit depth. Amarone is the dry wine made from grapes shrivelled on racks.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Etna is one of the southernmost vineyards in Europe, yet its reds come out pale and sharp. What allows that?
options: Sea breezes that cool the whole island evenly
Black volcanic ash reflecting sunlight away from the bunches
Picking in August, ahead of the worst of the heat
Vineyards climbing from about 400m to over 1000m on the volcano
cards.a: Height, on a mountain that is still building itself. Vines run from about 400m past 1000m up the flanks, so nights stay cold and the harvest can reach November. Nerello Mascalese, the main red grape, is thin-skinned and pale in the way Nebbiolo is, with acid and tannin but little colour.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why does the first Japanese green tea of the year nearly always come from Kagoshima rather than from Uji?
options: It lies at the southern end of Kyushu, on flat land planted with early cultivars
Its growers shade the bushes in winter to force an earlier bud break
Its bushes are a different species, one that wakes earlier
Its bushes are pruned in autumn instead of spring, so they wake sooner
cards.a: Spring arrives there first, and the fields are flat enough to plant early cultivars and cut them by machine. Uji sits far to the north on slopes and follows two or three weeks later, with Shizuoka further east again the biggest grower. A first tea tells you where it grew.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Burgundy's ladder runs regional, village, premier cru, grand cru. What may a grower do with fruit off a grand cru row?
options: Nothing else: fruit from a classified row must carry that row's name
Sell it under the neighbouring grand cru, if the two vineyards adjoin
Sell it under any name below its rank, but never above
Blend up to a fifth of it into a village wine and keep the higher rank
cards.a: The ladder only runs downward. Each step up covers less ground and caps the yield harder. A grower may always declassify into a name beneath his own, and never into one above it. That is why a village wine from a great address can drink so far above its label.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Since 2017 a Rioja label may read Viñedo Singular. What does that phrase certify?
options: A single grape variety, bottled without the usual blending partners
A vineyard the winery owns outright rather than buys fruit from
One named plot, old and cropped low, with the wine passed by tasting
A wine held back even longer than Gran Reserva before release
cards.a: An origin, not an ageing term. The 2017 rules built a ladder of place beside the old one: zone, then village, then a single plot at the top. That plot must be at least 35 years old, hand-picked, cropped well under the regional limit, and passed by two tastings.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A cooperative buys its members' grapes by weight. What does that do to the wine it makes?
options: Nothing rewards a smaller crop, so it comes out sound and anonymous
Members pick late, once the berries have shrivelled and lost weight
Members plant whichever varieties ripen earliest in the season
The best fruit goes into one cuvée and the rest is sold off in bulk
cards.a: A member is paid for what the trailer weighs, and cutting his crop to improve it costs him money. That is the structural reason so much cooperative wine is clean, cheap and anonymous. The ones that climbed out of it now grade fruit parcel by parcel and pay different rates for it.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: The Douro's terraces were planted for Port, so where do its dry red wines come from?
options: Port that failed to reach the sweetness required and was finished dry
Newer vineyards planted on cooler, higher ground away from the river
A separate set of grape varieties that may not legally be fortified
Fruit left over once a grower's annual Port allowance is filled
cards.a: Fruit that cannot legally become Port. Each year the trade body fixes how much of the harvest may be fortified, then shares that benefício out by a vineyard grade running A to F. Anything beyond a grower's share ferments dry instead. The same terraces make both.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Two Fujian white teas, one from Fuding and one from Zhenghe. What is chiefly making them taste different?
options: Whether the buds are picked before or after the leaf beside them opens
How much sun the leaf sees while it withers, and for how long
How far oxidation is allowed to run before heat is used to stop it
The age of the bushes the pickers are working
cards.a: White tea is almost entirely its wither, and the two places wither differently. Fuding is coastal and mild, and breaks the long air-drying with short spells of open sun: fresher, downier, sweeter. Zhenghe is inland, higher and colder, and withers under a roof: honey and dried dates.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Sun Moon Lake's Ruby 18 is a black tea that finishes cool and minty with nothing added to it. Where does that come from?
options: The lake fog, which slows growth through the last weeks before picking
Oxidation pushed further than in any other black tea
A slow charcoal roast given to the leaf after it is dried
One of its parents, a wild tea native to Taiwan's own forests
cards.a: A bred cultivar. It was crossed at a government station from a large-leaf Burmese plant and a wild Taiwanese mountain tea. The cool note comes down from that wild parent every harvest. Japan planted large-leaf tea at the lake in the 1920s, which is why black tea is made there.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A Burgundy label prints the word Monopole beneath the vineyard name. What does that change?
options: One estate owns the whole vineyard, so no rival bottling of it exists
One grower farms it under a lease from the many owners of the land
The wine may be sold only by the estate and never through a merchant
The estate owns every vine in the village, from regional land to cru
cards.a: Nearly every Burgundian cru is split between dozens of owners, so there is always a rival bottling off the same ground to judge a grower by. A monopole has one owner and one reading of the site, and nothing beside it to argue with. La Tâche and La Romanée are two.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A bottle of Vinho Verde is not green. So what is the verde describing?
options: Unripe grapes, picked deliberately short of full maturity
The green glass the region has always bottled in
The wine's youth: it is sold within months of the harvest
The granite the vines are rooted in across the north
cards.a: Verde means young rather than green. This is the far north of Portugal, and the wine goes out within months of picking, often at only 9 to 11% alcohol. The faint prickle began as an accident, a bacterial fermentation finishing in the bottle, and is now usually gas added at bottling.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why does a bottle of Pays d'Oc name its grape when a Minervois grown up the road does not?
options: Minervois is a blend, and only single-variety wines may name a grape
Pays d'Oc is made for export, where French labelling rules do not apply
The grapes in Minervois are not on France's list of permitted varieties
They sit in different tiers, and the looser one allows it
cards.a: Different tiers, different promises. An appellation such as Minervois fixes which varieties may be planted and in what proportion, and offers the place name as the guarantee, so the grape stays off the label. Pays d'Oc is an IGP, a looser tier, and it allows the grape.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A brick of Chinese dark tea is full of stalk and coarse old leaf that any other class would sort out. Why is it left in?
options: Stalk holds most of the caffeine, and the long ageing then removes it
It carries the sugars the microbes feed on through the fermentation
It bulks out the brick cheaply, and buyers are paying for weight
The stalk chars away during firing and leaves channels behind it
cards.a: The microbes need it. Coarse leaf and stem hold the sugars and fibre that the fungi and bacteria of a dark tea pile actually feed on. So the grade is a specification, not a corner cut. Tender buds would starve the process. A Fu brick may legally run near a fifth stalk.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Some teas are boiled in a pan rather than steeped in a pot. Which ones, and why?
options: Delicate spring buds, which will not open in still water
Broken leaf and dust, which need the movement to give up their colour
Coarse mature leaf and old pressed tea, which a short steep barely opens
Heavily roasted leaf, to drive off the last of the char
cards.a: Mature leaf and stalk are woody, and years under the press shut a cake tighter still, so five minutes in hot water takes very little out of either. A rolling boil pulls the sugars and the body through. It is how butter tea is made on the Tibetan plateau.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Rolled black tea leaf is set aside to oxidise. What is the maker controlling while it does?
options: The room's temperature and damp, and how deep the leaf is heaped
How much air is blown through the pile, and nothing besides
The weight pressing down on the leaf as it changes colour
How much water is sprayed on to keep the leaf pliable
cards.a: Oxidation gives off its own heat, so a deep bed cooks itself. The leaf goes into a cool, damp room in thin layers for an hour or two. The maker reads the colour and the smell, then fires it hard to stop it. Run too warm and the tea comes out flat and stewed.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: White tea's cheapest grade, Shou Mei, is the one most often laid down for years. Why not the buds?
options: Buds are too fragile to survive being pressed into a cake
Buds have lost their sweetness already by the time they are dried
The coarse grade holds more moisture, and ageing needs it
Mature leaf carries more of the material that ageing works on
cards.a: Shou Mei is the late, large-leaf picking, and mature leaf holds far more sugar and polysaccharide than a bud, so there is more in it to change: years take it toward jujube, honey and something medicinal. A bud is prized for what it is now, and time mostly costs it that.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Enshi Yulu in Hubei is steamed rather than fired in a pan, which almost no other Chinese green tea is. Why does it stand alone?
options: Steaming was China's older method, and this is where it is still used
The local leaf is too tender to be handled in a hot pan
The garden was set up by Japanese growers in the last century
Steaming is the only way to hold a leaf in a needle shape
cards.a: Steaming is how the Tang fixed green tea. Japan took the method and kept it, while China turned to the wok. Enshi Yulu is the one steamed Chinese green made at any scale, and it arrives as a dark jade needle, drinking closer to a sencha than to its neighbours.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: In Myanmar tea is eaten as well as drunk. What has been done to the leaf on the plate?
options: It is dried, powdered and stirred into oil
It is packed away from the air and soured by bacteria
It is boiled down to a paste with salt and sugar
It is the wet leaf left behind after brewing
cards.a: Laphet is pickled. Steamed leaf is pressed hard into a pit or a bamboo tube to shut the air out. Lactic bacteria and yeasts then sour it over months, the way they sour cabbage. It reaches the table savoury and tart, with fried beans, garlic and sesame.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Water boils at about 93C two thousand metres up. What does that do to a tightly rolled oolong brewed there?
options: It extracts faster, because the lower pressure drives water into the leaf
It scorches the leaf less, so the tea comes out sweeter than at sea level
The ball opens slowly, so the early steeps run thin unless they are given longer
Nothing at all: the leaf only registers that the water is boiling
cards.a: Boiling point falls with air pressure, so a kettle on Lishan, at 1600m in Taiwan, tops out near 93C and cannot be pushed past it. A hard ball of leaf needs heat to unfurl, so it opens late and the first infusions come out weak. More leaf, or longer pours, is the answer.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A squeeze of lemon goes over the fish, and the wine that worked a minute ago tastes flat. What has the acid on the plate done?
options: It has stripped out the wine's fruit and left its acid standing bare
It has lowered the acidity you read in the wine, so a soft wine goes flabby
It has raised the wine's apparent alcohol, so the wine reads hot
It has numbed the tongue, so nothing tasted after it registers properly
cards.a: Acid in the dish lowers the acidity you register in the glass, and pushes the wine's fruit and body forward. So a soft wine goes flabby and a sharp one is rescued. The working rule: the wine needs at least as much acid as the food.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A hot curry beside a ripe red at 15%. Why does the burn get worse rather than better?
options: Tannin binds the chilli oil and holds it against the palate
The chilli has numbed the tongue, so only the alcohol still registers
Ethanol acts on the same receptor as chilli heat, so it adds to the burn
Alcohol dries the mouth out, and a dry mouth feels heat more sharply
cards.a: Alcohol lands on the same receptor. Capsaicin, the compound behind chilli heat, is read by one that also answers to ethanol, so alcohol stacks onto the burn instead of washing it away. Sugar and cold damp it down, which is why an off-dry Riesling at 9% copes.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why does a hard, tannic red read softer against a fatty cut of beef than it does on its own?
options: Fat raises the mouth's pH, and tannin binds less in a neutral mouth
The fat coats the tongue and blocks the taste buds, so less registers
Chewing raises saliva, and the extra saliva simply dilutes the wine
Astringency is felt as friction, and fat lays back the film tannin strips away
cards.a: Astringency is not a taste but a drag: tannin disrupts the slippery film that keeps the surfaces of the mouth sliding, and you feel the friction. Fat lays that film back down. So the richness has to be real, and a lean fillet does far less than a fatty rib.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: The local wine with the local dish is the oldest advice in wine. What is that rule actually worth?
options: It is convention: generations ate and drank the two together and kept what worked
The same soil grew both, so the flavours share a common origin
It is folklore, and only the sugar, acid and fat on the plate decide anything
Regional wines are made deliberately to suit the regional cooking
cards.a: It is a tested habit rather than a mechanism, and nothing about shared soil is doing the work. So it fails wherever either side has moved since. Tomatoes reached Italy after Columbus, and Chianti today is a different wine from the one the habit grew around.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A taster holds the wine, swallows, then breathes out through the nose. Why not simply sniff the glass harder?
options: The mouth warms the wine, so it gives up compounds a cool glass never released
The back of the nose holds a second and more sensitive set of receptors
Repeated sniffing tires the nose, so the mouth is used as a substitute
Swallowing clears the sinuses, so the sniff that follows registers more
cards.a: Flavour is mostly smell, and smell has two doors: in at the nostrils, and up the back of the throat from the mouth, the retronasal route. Warmed to body temperature, the wine gives up heavier compounds a cool glass never released. So the finish smells unlike the nose.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A taster calls one wine intense and the next one long. What is each of those words measuring?
options: Intensity is the aroma on the nose, length is the flavour in the mouth
Intensity is how loud the wine is, length is how long it holds after swallowing
Intensity is the alcohol, and length is the acidity carrying it
They are one thing under two names, used at opposite ends of the palate
cards.a: Two separate clocks. Intensity is how loud the wine is while it is in the mouth; length is how many seconds the flavour holds after you swallow, and finish is the character of what stays. A loud oaky red can be short and a quiet Riesling long.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A tasting note says a wine has structure and says nothing at all about fruit. What has that word named?
options: The parts you feel rather than smell: acid, tannin, alcohol and any sugar
The wine's capacity to age, which is what the taster is really predicting
The weight and texture that oak and ageing added to it
The balance between the fruit on the nose and the fruit on the palate
cards.a: Structure is the frame you feel rather than smell: acid, tannin, alcohol and any sugar. Aroma and fruit are the flesh over it. Balance is those two in proportion, not the components being low, so a bone dry, hard, sharp wine can be perfectly balanced.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A shop sells a different glass for every grape. What does the shape of a glass reliably change?
options: Where the wine lands on the tongue, and so which tastes come forward
How much surface the wine evaporates from, and where that vapour is funnelled
How fast the wine takes up oxygen, and so how quickly it opens up
How long the wine holds its temperature, which the thickness decides
cards.a: Aroma, in two steps. The bowl sets how much surface the wine can evaporate from, and the taper decides how much of that vapour is funnelled to your nose. So how far you fill it counts as much as its shape: filled to the brim, a glass collects nothing.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Reds at room temperature, whites from the fridge. What is wrong with following that as written?
options: Fridges run colder than their dial says, so a white arrives near freezing
Room temperature meant an unheated house, and a glass warms but never cools
It holds for red and fails for white, since whites want no chilling at all
It ignores the grape, and grape rather than style is what sets the temperature
cards.a: Room temperature is a phrase from houses nobody heated, nearer 16C than a modern 21C. So most reds reach the table too warm, and most whites too cold. Traffic in the glass runs one way as well: it warms in the hand and never cools. Err cold.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Half a bottle is left over. What actually decides whether it is still worth drinking in three days?
options: The closure, since a screwcap reseals where a cork no longer does
Whether it was decanted, because a decanted wine has spent its oxygen already
How much air the wine is left in contact with, and how cold it is kept
Its alcohol, since alcohol is what preserves a wine against spoilage
cards.a: Oxidation, and its rate is set by the area of wine meeting air and by temperature. So the two moves that work are cutting the headspace, by pouring what is left into a smaller bottle, and refrigerating it, reds included. Delicate whites and old reds go first.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A wine cellar is kept damp, at around 70% humidity. Why, when the wine is sealed inside glass?
options: It stops the labels drying out and lifting away from the glass
Damp air conducts heat badly, so the cellar holds its temperature more steadily
Moist air is the heavier, so it settles and keeps the bottles cool
Dry air shrinks the outer end of the cork, and a shrunk cork lets air in
cards.a: The wine is sealed in glass but the cork is not: its outer end sits in the room. Dry air pulls water out of it and it shrinks away from the neck, which is also why bottles lie down, to keep the inner end wet. A screwcap wants none of this.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Most wine is at its best on release. What does the small minority that improves in bottle actually have?
options: Concentration, which is why low yields and old vines are the usual sign
Enough alcohol to hold off spoilage while the flavours knit together
A reserve of acid, tannin or sugar, since fruit is what time spends first
Good oak, because ageing in bottle carries on what the barrel started
cards.a: Fruit is the part time takes away, so a wine needs something left standing once it has gone: acid, tannin, sugar, or the spirit in a fortified one. Nothing fattens in bottle. A wine that is thin now will only ever be thin and old later.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A German white comes in a squat flattened flask instead of a tall bottle. What does that shape tell you?
options: It is a sweet wine, and the flask sets it apart on the shelf
It is Franken, whose flask is protected in law, and the wine will be dry
It holds a litre rather than 75cl, which the flask carries more neatly
It is Riesling, since the flask is reserved for Germany's flagship grape
cards.a: The Bocksbeutel belongs to Franken and its use is protected in EU law. Franken is Germany's most continental region, hard winters and an early autumn, so its grape is Silvaner rather than late-ripening Riesling, and the wine is nearly always dry and savoury.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Zweigelt was made at an Austrian research station in 1922 by crossing two local grapes. What was the breeder after?
options: A vine that would survive the phylloxera louse without being grafted
Deeper colour, since both of the parent grapes make pale wine
A ripening calendar: budding later than one parent, ripening before the other
Cold tolerance, so that Austria could plant red vines much further north
cards.a: A crossing is two varieties of one species bred on purpose. St. Laurent buds early and meets spring frost; Blaufränkisch, the dark peppery Austrian red, ripens so late autumn rain catches it. Zweigelt buds after one and ripens before the other, and is Austria's most planted red.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A German shelf carries Spätburgunder, Weissburgunder and Grauburgunder side by side. What are those three?
options: Pinot Noir, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris, one family under German names
Three picking dates for one grape: late, white-ripe and grey-ripe
Three Burgundian imports: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Aligoté
Three clones of Pinot Noir, sorted by the colour of the finished wine
cards.a: Pinot Noir, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris, which are one variety and two colour mutations of it. Burgunder names the family and spät means late, for the red's ripening. Germany is now the world's third-largest grower of Pinot Noir, mostly in Baden and the Ahr.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Blaufränkisch buds early and ripens late, which is the worst pair of habits a vine can have. Where does Austria grow it?
options: In the far west, on Alpine foothills where the growing season opens earliest
On the Wachau's stone terraces, which hold the day's heat through the night
Hardly at all: it is a German and Hungarian grape that Austria mostly imports
In Burgenland, on the hot plain in the east, where the autumn runs longest
cards.a: Burgenland, on the Pannonian plain around the Neusiedlersee, where hot dry summers run into long warm autumns: the season this grape needs to finish at all. It is Lemberger in Germany and Kékfrankos in Hungary, and it pours dark and firm with high acid and a peppery edge.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Cava is Spain's bottle-fermented sparkling wine. Which part of Spain does the name point to?
options: Penedès in Catalonia, to which the name is legally reserved
Rioja, where the method arrived from France in the 1870s
Nowhere at all, since any Spanish sparkling wine may use the word
Scattered zones across four regions, though nearly all of it is Catalan
cards.a: Almost all of it, oddly. Cava was defined by how it is made rather than where, so the name reaches municipalities from Catalonia out to Rioja, Aragón, Valencia and Extremadura, now in four zones. Ageing is the ladder: nine months, eighteen for Reserva, thirty for Gran Reserva.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Spain's old Garnacha vineyards are nearly all on high, poor, awkward ground. Why is that where the old vines are left?
options: Garnacha fell from fashion, and only land too awkward to replant was spared
Garnacha will not root on deep fertile soil, so it was never planted there
Phylloxera never climbed to the high sites, so those vines are the originals
The oldest vines were protected by law once their age was recognised
cards.a: Fashion and subsidy. Garnacha was written off as bulk wine and pulled out through the 1990s for Tempranillo and French varieties, and what got replanted was the flat, irrigable ground. What nobody bothered to pull sits high and poor, which is where the grape is good.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A Japanese tea farm plants Saemidori and Okumidori in among its Yabukita. What is that mixture for?
options: Blending, since the three are always mixed to a house flavour before sale
Frost insurance, because one of the three will always come through a bad spring
Disease, since a field of a single clone would go down to one outbreak
Time: they bud a week either side of Yabukita, which spreads the picking out
cards.a: Fresh leaf has to be steamed the day it is cut, so a field that comes ready all at once is more than a farm can handle. Saemidori buds about five days early and Okumidori some ten days late, so the harvest runs over weeks. The late one dodges frost as well.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A Taiwanese oolong is offered as dong pian, and the seller says there was none at all last year. What is it?
options: The last of the previous crop, sold off before the spring leaf arrives
Leaf from bushes left unpicked in autumn, so it is already a year old
A shoot pushed after the winter harvest, when a warm spell breaks dormancy
The lowest grade of the winter picking, sorted out and sold under its own name
cards.a: Winter sprout. Above 1000m the bush shuts down after the November picking, but a mild December can trick it into pushing one more flush, cut before the spring crop. Some years it comes and some it does not, so dong pian is a one-off rather than a grade.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Milk suits a strong Assam and wrecks a jasmine green. What is it doing to the delicate tea?
options: It cools the cup below the temperature that carries aroma
Its fat dissolves the aromatics and holds them back from your nose
It lifts the pH of the liquor, which flattens the floral notes
It coats the tongue, so the tea's own sweetness never registers
cards.a: Fat traps the aroma. Most of what a scented tea smells of is oil soluble, so milk fat takes those compounds into itself and far less reaches the air above the cup. A strong black tea still has colour, body and grip left. A perfumed one is mostly the perfume.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A pinch of salt takes the bitterness out of a tea that brewed too hard. What is it doing?
options: Salt binds the bitter compounds and drops them out of the liquor
Sodium suppresses how much bitterness is registered at all
Salt lifts the liquor's pH, which converts the bitter compounds
Salt makes the mouth water, and that saliva dilutes the cup
cards.a: Sodium interferes with the way bitterness is registered. So it takes bitterness away rather than covering it over, and it works well below the level at which you would taste salt at all. Cooks use the same trick on grapefruit and on coffee.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Wherever tea is drunk heavily sweetened it is also brewed unusually strong. Why do those two habits travel together?
options: Sugar slows extraction, so the leaf needs far longer in the water
Strong tea holds its colour once milk and sugar are both in it
Sugar damps bitterness and grip, so the leaf can be brewed harder
Sweetened tea is drunk cooler, and a cool cup always reads weaker
cards.a: Sugar dissolved in the tea itself suppresses both bitterness and the dry grip of astringency, which lifts the ceiling on how hard the leaf can be pushed. Moroccan mint tea, masala chai and Turkish tea are all built on that trade.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A sushi counter serves a big mug of coarse, scalding green tea at the end of the meal and never the good leaf. What is that tea for?
options: Heat and grip to clear fish fat, in a leaf too cheap to compete with the food
Its caffeine, which is held to settle the stomach after raw fish
A courtesy signal that the meal is over and the bill is on its way
Scalding water, which is there to kill anything the raw fish carried
cards.a: It is deliberately coarse: the dust sorted out of sencha during refining, brewed scalding. Fat sets on a cool mouth and a hot drying liquor clears it, which is the job. A delicate tea would be lost against soy and vinegar anyway. The tea is agari, the dust konacha.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A taster calls one tea strong but thin and the next light but thick. Is that a contradiction?
options: Yes, thickness is only another word for strength in the cup
No: thickness is judged on the wet leaf and strength in the liquor
Yes, unless the two of them were brewed at different temperatures
No: strength is what you pulled out, thickness is what the leaf had
cards.a: Concentration is set by the brewer with leaf, water and time. The weight and coating a liquor has in the mouth is not, and comes largely from soluble sugars and polysaccharides the leaf built. Chinese tasters keep the words apart: nong for strong, hou for thick.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: In Taiwan a tall narrow cup is set beside the drinking cup and you are told not to drink from it. What is it for?
options: A measure, so that every guest at the table is poured the same
Keeping the next infusion hot while the first one is drunk
The tea goes in and is tipped straight out, and you smell the empty cup
Holding the rinse, so the pot can be warmed through twice
cards.a: Tea is poured in, the drinking cup inverted over it and the pair turned so the tall one drains. What is left is a warm film with a lot of surface and no liquid holding it back, so it reads loud and keeps shifting for a minute. It is the aroma cup, wen xiang bei.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Tasters let a cup go cold before they decide on a tea. What does cooling expose?
options: Sweetness fades much faster on cooling than bitterness does
Cold thickens the liquor, which makes weight in the mouth easier to judge
The tannins settle out of a cold cup and leave the aromatics on their own
A cold tongue works more slowly, so each flavour lasts longer on it
cards.a: Sweetness falls away far faster than bitterness and grip do as a cup cools, and the aromatics that were lifting off the hot liquor stop arriving. A cold cup is the tea with its flattery removed, and one still sweet cold has something real underneath.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A Chinese green tea is sold as ming qian, picked before the Qingming festival around 4 April. Why is that date worth less than it looks?
options: Qingming falls later the further north a garden happens to lie
Before Qingming the leaf must be picked by hand, and after it by machine
Only gardens in Zhejiang are entitled to use the term at all
A fixed date, and no two gardens are at the same point of their season
cards.a: Qingming is a calendar date and the bush does not know it. A warm southern lowland garden is well into its flush by then, and a high cold one may not have moved at all. The words rank pickings within one garden and mean very little across two.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A pack of Indian black tea says orthodox. What is that word describing?
options: One garden: an orthodox tea is never blended with any other
Hand work: an orthodox tea is rolled without any machinery
The machine: rollers twist and press the leaf whole
Purity: no flavouring of any kind may be added to an orthodox tea
cards.a: Orthodox names the machine, not the garden. Rollers twist and press whole leaf the way hands once did, and how hard they press is a dial: light for a floral Darjeeling, hard for a strong Assam. One batch comes off in many sizes and is sifted into grades.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Two Chardonnays spend a year in the same new oak barrels and one tastes far more of oak. What did the other do differently?
options: It fermented in the barrel, so the yeast worked on the wood compounds
It was racked off its lees before the barrel ageing ever began
Its barrels were filled fuller, so less air ever reached the wine
It was bottled straight out of a much colder cellar than the other
cards.a: Barrel fermentation puts the ferment inside the wood. Yeast turns vanillin, the compound behind the vanilla note, into a far quieter one, and the lees take up wood tannin as they settle. Ferment in steel first and the oak lands on top of the wine, not into it.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Carignan was pulled up across southern France as bulk-wine material and is now sought out there as old vines. What changed about it?
options: Clonal selection eventually produced a better-behaved version of the grape
Warmer summers now ripen it, where in the 1970s it never reached ripeness at all
The appellations lifted the cap that had kept it out of serious wine
Nothing: it is a late, hugely vigorous vine, and only a small crop lets it finish
cards.a: Carignan will carry an enormous crop and ripens very late, so the south planted it by the hectare and the wine came out hard, sharp and hollow. Old bush vines on poor schist crop a fraction of that and do ripen, and the grape then pours dark and savoury.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A Bordeaux château sells its grand vin, the wine under the château's own name, and a second wine beside it. What decides which lots go where?
options: The second wine comes off a separate, lesser vineyard the estate also owns
