It is the same blend, simply bottled younger and without any oak on it
A selection at blending: young vines, weak parcels and the hardest lots
It carries the fruit the estate buys in from its neighbours each year
cards.a: Selection. Young vines, parcels that underperformed and the hard wine pressed from the drained skins are all held out, so the grand vin can be chosen more tightly. That is why second wines spread as standards rose, and why one can drink well, and early.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A wine list offers a red Sancerre. What grape is in it, and why is it not the one Sancerre is famous for?
options: Pinot Noir: the eastern Loire grew red until the vineyard was replanted
Cabernet Franc, which makes the reds everywhere else along the Loire
Gamay, held over from when the region shipped its wine to Paris
Malbec, going by Côt, its old name in the Loire
cards.a: Sancerre is one appellation in three colours, and its red and rosé must be Pinot Noir. It lies nearer Burgundy than the Atlantic and was largely red until phylloxera, the root-eating aphid, wiped the vineyard out and Sauvignon Blanc went back in its place.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A tea bought loose from an open jar in a shop tastes faintly of that shop once you get it home. What has happened to it?
options: The lid trapped moisture, and the leaf has started to oxidise in the jar
Light through the glass has bleached the aromatics out of the leaf
Scooping has broken the leaf and released stale dust into the packet
Dry leaf is porous and oily, and takes up whatever is in the air
cards.a: Dry tea is porous and coated in its own oils, and it takes up the smells around it within days. That is exactly the property jasmine scenting uses on purpose. So keep tea away from spices, coffee and a shared fridge, and be wary of an open jar.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: The tea year in Japan's tea ceremony opens in November, with leaf that was picked the previous May. Where has it been?
options: Ageing in cedar, which is what gives ceremony matcha its wood note
Travelling to Kyoto by the old road, a journey that once took months
Fermenting slowly, the way Japan's rarest teas are made
Sealed whole in a jar, unmilled, resting right through the summer
cards.a: The leaf matcha is ground from goes whole into a sealed jar in spring and is opened in November, and only then milled. Six months shut away rounds the sharpness off. It rests whole because ground matcha only goes stale. Cutting that seal opens the tea year: kuchikiri.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A tin says Uji tea. How much does that name promise about where the leaf grew?
options: All of it: the leaf has to be grown in Uji city itself
Only the cultivar, which must be one of the lines bred at Uji
Little: leaf from four prefectures qualifies, so long as Kyoto finished it
Nothing at all, because Uji names a way of making tea rather than a place
cards.a: The Kyoto trade defines Uji tea as leaf grown in Kyoto, Nara, Shiga or Mie and then refined inside Kyoto: sorted, blended and fired by a Kyoto house. Uji itself is small and largely built over. The name promises the finishing hand rather than the field.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A Taiwanese oolong is sold as gaoshan, high mountain. Is there a height it has to clear?
options: No law sets one: 1000m is the trade's habit, not a rule
1000m, checked and certified by Taiwan's agriculture ministry
It must come from one of five named mountains, whatever their height
800m, the point above which the bushes can no longer be machine-picked
cards.a: Gaoshan is a market word with no legal floor under it, and 1000m is convention rather than rule. Height is a stand-in for cloud, cold nights and slow growth, and a stand-in can be wrong: a cool shaded site below the line can beat a bare sunny one above it.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A Darjeeling pack names the garden, then reads DJ-12, 2025. What is that number?
options: The grade, on a numbered scale that Darjeeling uses by itself
The batch: one day's picking, numbered in sequence through the season
The number of the plot within the garden that the leaf was picked from
The auction lot it was bought in, which is what fixed its price
cards.a: Gardens sell by invoice, and DJ is simply Darjeeling. A day's leaf off one section becomes a few chests, numbered in order from the season's start, so DJ-12 is early. It is a date stamp and not a score: a later lot off better weather can beat it.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Assam's first flush is thin and its second flush is the one sold by name. What does late May bring that March does not?
options: A change of pluckers, from the machines back to hand picking
The monsoon, and the plant only gets heat and water together once it breaks
Cooler nights, which slow the bush down and concentrate the leaf
A second pruning, which forces a heavier shoot out of the bush
cards.a: The rains. Assam's March crop grows through a dry, cool spring and comes out light and brisk. The monsoon breaks in late May, and the large-leaf bush finally has the heat and water it is built for. That flush is the dark, malty tea with golden tips.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Burgundy's grand crus sit in a band partway up the slope, never at the top and never at the bottom. What is wrong with each end?
options: The top is too steep to plant and the bottom floods most springs
The top is thin and cold, the bottom deep, damp and frost-prone
The top faces the wrong way and the bottom is shaded by the hill
The top and bottom were planted later, once the middle filled up
cards.a: Mid-slope is the compromise. Above it the soil thins toward bare rock and the wind and cold bite. Below it the washed-down soil is deep and fertile, holds water, and cold air pools there on a spring night. The band between drains freely, warms early and keeps just enough soil.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: The Médoc has a saying that the best vines see the river. What is the Gironde actually doing for them?
options: Reflecting light back up onto the bunches on the near bank
Carrying the barrels out, which is why the trade settled there
Draining the gravel banks, which would otherwise waterlog
Damping the temperature swings, and spring frost above all
cards.a: A large body of water warms and cools slowly, so it holds off spring frost and takes the edge off a heat spike. The gravel is the same story: the river laid those banks down, so the deepest and best-draining of them lie nearest it. The saying tracks two things at once.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: In Châteauneuf-du-Pape, in the southern Rhône, the best-known vineyards are carpeted in big round stones. What do those galets do?
options: Reflect sunlight up into the canopy from underneath
Store the day's heat, and cover the soil against evaporation
Feed the vine minerals as they slowly break down
Keep pickers off the soil, so it never compacts
cards.a: Two things at once: they take up heat through the day and give it back overnight, and they cap the soil so less water evaporates out of it. Not every fine parcel has them, which is the catch. Some of the best sites are deep sand, and those give the perfumed, lighter wines.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A Barolo label prints Cannubi or Bussia under the appellation. Is that a cru in the Burgundian sense?
options: Yes: the zone was ranked, and these are the vineyards at its top
No: the names are delimited, but not one is ranked above another
No: they are the producer's own brand names for a bottling
Yes, but only the eleven communes may be printed, never a plot
cards.a: Barolo mapped and named 170 vineyards in 2010, plus its eleven communes. The boundary is official and the yield is cut a little, but the list is deliberately flat: nothing in the rules says one site beats another. The hierarchy is real and it lives in the market, not in law.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: White tea is sold as the gentle, low-caffeine one. Is it?
options: No: a bud-only white can out-caffeinate a strong black tea
Yes: the leaf is barely handled, so less caffeine is ever freed
Yes, but only because it is normally brewed cooler and shorter
No: caffeine runs the same in every class, since it is one plant
cards.a: Caffeine is the plant's own insecticide and it is concentrated in the youngest growth, so a bud-only Silver Needle can carry more than a coarse black tea. The class tells you almost nothing. Leaf age, cultivar, water temperature and steep length are what decide the cup.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Why does a puerh cake's outer leaf often look better than what a pick pulls out of the middle?
options: The outside meets the air, so it darkens to a handsomer colour
Pressing drives the finer leaf outward and the stalk inward
Cakes can be faced: better leaf is laid in the mould first
The face is brushed with a finishing spray before wrapping
cards.a: Some cakes are faced. A layer of better leaf goes into the mould before the body follows, so the surface is not a sample of the whole. That is why buyers pry from a broken edge rather than the face, and why a serious seller will hand you a cake already opened.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Two brews of one leaf come out equally strong: more leaf briefly, or less leaf for longer. Do they taste alike?
options: Yes: the same amount has dissolved into the water either way
No: the short steep is the thinner one whatever the ratio
No: the longer steep carries proportionally more bitterness
Yes, unless the water temperature differed between the two
cards.a: Compounds leave the leaf at different rates. Amino acids and simple sugars come out early and then level off; catechins and caffeine keep climbing the longer the leaf sits. Matching strength with time buys the same intensity with more bitterness underneath it.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: German ripeness levels climb from Kabinett up to Trockenbeerenauslese. What is the picker doing differently at the top?
options: Waiting later into the autumn, and nothing else changes
Freezing the fruit, so the water can be taken off as ice
Pressing harder, so that more sugar comes out of the skins
Selecting: whole bunches, then single berries, then shrivelled ones
cards.a: The ladder measures sugar in the grape, and above Spätlese it is bought by sorting. Auslese means selected bunches, Beerenauslese selected berries, Trockenbeerenauslese shrivelled ones taken singly. Eiswein sits outside it: whole frozen berries, pressed while the water is ice.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Why does a tannic red genuinely feel softer after fifteen years?
options: Most of the tannin drops out as sediment, so less is left
The tannin changes structure and binds saliva less readily
The acidity falls, so the tannin reads rounder against it
Alcohol escapes through the cork, uncovering the fruit
cards.a: Not by leaving. Thirty and fifty year verticals show aged reds holding tannin concentrations close to young ones, so precipitation is not the main story. The tannin itself rearranges into forms that bind salivary protein weakly, and weak binding is what the mouth reads as soft.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Côte-Rôtie co-ferments up to a fifth of white Viognier with its Syrah. Tradition says this fixes the colour. Does it?
options: Yes: Viognier skins carry a cofactor that stabilises red pigment
No: trials find it flat or paler, and aroma is the real gain
Yes, but only co-fermented, never blended in afterwards
No: it is done for alcohol, since Viognier ripens after Syrah
cards.a: Co-fermentation is the tradition and copigmentation the theory, but trials find no colour benefit and a loss at high proportions. What survives is an aromatic lift, real but more modest than the story around it. Viognier also ripens before Syrah, not after.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A quick first steep is poured away to cut the caffeine. Roughly how much does that take out?
options: Almost all of it, since caffeine dissolves out first
A fifth at most, and often a good deal less
About half of it, which is the usual claim
None at all, since caffeine needs a long steep
cards.a: Caffeine comes out early but nowhere near completely. Estimates for a rinse of a few seconds up to half a minute run from under a tenth to about a fifth, and none is a direct measurement. Losing half needs minutes of steeping thrown away, and the flavour goes too.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Chinese tea grading scores five things and adds them up. Why is an oolong not scored the same way as a green tea?
options: It is: one rubric covers every category equally
The five scores are weighted differently by category
Oolong is scored on three factors, green tea on five
Oolong is scored by a panel, green tea by one taster
cards.a: The weights move. Appearance, liquor colour, aroma, taste and leaf base are each scored, then multiplied: roughly 25/10/25/30/10 for green tea, 20/5/30/35/5 for oolong. Aroma and taste carry 65% of an oolong because that is what the category is for.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A Chinese evaluator smells the same tea three times as it cools. What does each pass catch?
options: Hot shows the top notes and any scorch, cool shows what persists
Nothing new: it only confirms the first impression
Hot shows the taste, warm the aroma, cool the body
Each pass is a different taster, to average the judgement
cards.a: Volatiles leave at different temperatures, so one sniff reads one fraction. Hot brings the top notes and any scorching; warm gives the tea's own character at its fullest; cool shows what persists, and the staleness or muddiness that heat was covering.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: The Chinese standard judges green tea on one five-minute steep and oolong on three. Why the difference?
options: Oolong leaf is too tightly rolled to open in one steep
Three steeps average out an uneven roast
Oolong is graded on how it holds up across infusions
Oolong needs three to reach the same strength
cards.a: Endurance is part of the grade. Five grams sit in a 110ml covered bowl and are poured at roughly one, one and a half and two minutes, and the tea is reassessed after each. A tea that is loud once and hollow by the third pour has told the grader something.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A grader spreads the brewed leaf out, looks at it, then presses it between finger and thumb. What is the pressing for?
options: Feeling the pliability, which is itself scored
Checking that the leaf has fully brewed out
Testing for grit, which would mean poor sorting
Cooling it enough to smell it safely
cards.a: Leaf base is a scored factor and it is read by touch as well as by eye. Soft and springy says tender leaf, handled well; brittle or hard says over-firing or coarse material. Colour at the margin says how far oxidation ran. Western cupping rarely scores any of it.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: China holds tea people to two separate professional standards rather than one ladder. What splits them?
options: Level: one is simply the junior grade of the other
State employees against private practitioners
Green tea specialists against dark tea specialists
Judging tea against performing and serving it
cards.a: Two trades, two exams. The evaluator scores a tea against a written standard: appearance, liquor, aroma, taste, leaf base. The tea-art practitioner is examined on ceremony, ware, the tea table and service. Western sommelier courses fold a thin version of both into one.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Most Kenyan and Ceylon tea is sold through auction rooms in Mombasa and Colombo. What does that do to the tea itself?
options: Only the price: how it is sold leaves the tea unchanged
It fixes the picking date, since the auctions run weekly
It is built to hit a known grade a buyer can bid on blind
It guarantees the garden, since lots may not be blended
cards.a: A buyer bids off a small sample and a grade name, often without tasting widely. So leaf has to be made to hit that grade reliably, rather than to be interesting. It is much of why CTC dominates Kenya, and why a garden's identity survives better sold direct.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Most Kenyan tea comes off farms of an acre or two rather than estates. What does that do to how it is judged?
options: It varies wildly, since no two farms pick alike
Leaf is pooled at a shared factory, so the factory is the unit
It is picked younger, since small farms cannot wait
It is organic by default, since inputs cost too much
cards.a: Smallholders deliver green leaf to a shared factory within hours of picking, so hundreds of farms become one batch. The factory, not the farm, is what a buyer names and judges, and quality moves with processing rather than with any one garden.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Puerh, Dian Hong and China's wild tea forests all come out of Yunnan. What does that province have that the eastern ones do not?
options: A subtropical monsoon the eastern provinces lack
A dry season long enough to sun-dry every crop
Volcanic soil, which the east has almost none of
Big-leaf assamica growing wild, and old seed-grown trees
cards.a: The plant. Yunnan is where large-leaf assamica grows wild, in forest rather than hedge, and where seed-grown trees of real age still stand. The eastern provinces work small-leaf sinensis in clipped plantations. One species, a different plant, a different tea.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Cabernet Sauvignon is the most planted grape on earth. What makes it travel so well?
options: It ripens early, so it finishes in almost any climate
It keeps a recognisable signature across very different climates
It shrugs off the fungal diseases that limit other varieties
It crops heavily, so it pays wherever it is planted
cards.a: It holds its shape. Thick skins and small berries give colour, tannin and acid almost anywhere. The aroma runs a legible line too: green pepper when underripe, then blackcurrant, then cassis and cedar when ripe. Growers get a wine buyers recognise.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One Champagne says Blanc de Blancs and the next Blanc de Noirs, and both pour pale gold. What differs?
options: The grapes: all white, against black grapes pressed off their skins
The dosage, since Blanc de Noirs is always the drier
The lees ageing, which runs far longer for Blanc de Noirs
The vineyard rank, Blanc de Blancs being grand cru only
cards.a: Which of the three grapes went in. Blanc de Blancs is Chardonnay alone, taut and citrus-driven, and it ages long. Blanc de Noirs is Pinot Noir and Meunier pressed gently enough that no colour comes off the skins: broader and redder-fruited. Most Champagne blends all three.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Marlborough and Central Otago both make New Zealand Pinot Noir. Why do the two taste so unalike?
options: Otago is warmer overall, so its fruit is simply riper
Marlborough ferments whole bunches and Otago does not
Otago is continental on schist; Marlborough maritime on gravel
Otago plants a different clone, selected for the far south
cards.a: Climate shape and ground. Central Otago is the country's only continental region, inland, hot by day and cold by night on free-draining schist: dense, dark-fruited, structured. Marlborough is maritime on alluvial gravel, and gives lighter, herbal, red-fruited Pinot.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Pinotage was bred at the Cape in 1925 by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsault. What was the breeder trying to fix?
options: Cinsault's pale colour, which Pinot Noir would deepen
Both parents' low yields, which a crossing would raise
Cinsault's late ripening, which Pinot would pull earlier
Pinot Noir's fragility: its character on a hardier vine
cards.a: Abraham Perold, the Cape's first professor of viticulture, wanted Pinot Noir's quality on a vine that could take the heat and disease there. Cinsault, known locally as Hermitage, was hardy and reliable. The cross ripens early, and pushes a banana or acetone note when the ferment runs warm.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Coonawarra is a narrow strip of red soil over limestone in a flat, cool corner of South Australia. Why Cabernet?
options: Draining loam on limestone, in a climate cool enough for Cabernet
Iron in the red soil, which deepens the wine's colour
It is Australia's only region warm enough to finish Cabernet
Limestone lifts the soil pH, which softens Cabernet's tannin
cards.a: Terra rossa: a thin band of red clay loam over limestone, barely a dozen kilometres long. It drains freely and the site is cool for Australia, so Cabernet holds acidity and a leafy, minty lift over its blackcurrant. Warmer, lower Barossa Shiraz goes the other way.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: In Priorat, inland from Barcelona, old Garnacha and Carinena vines climb steep slopes of crumbling black slate. What does that ground do?
options: Reflects heat back up, which is what ripens the fruit
Forces roots deep for water, and the crop comes out tiny
Holds winter rain, so the vines never need irrigating
Adds its own mineral flavour straight into the wine
cards.a: Llicorella, a friable slate that roots can split. Water sits deep and nowhere else, so vines drive down for it and carry very little fruit. The wine comes out concentrated, high in alcohol and firm, which is why Priorat sits at a price its neighbours do not.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Soave is one of Italy's best-known white appellations and its grape is Garganega. What does Garganega actually bring?
options: A loud, grapey aroma, in the way that Muscat does
Very high sugar, which is why Soave finishes strong
Almond and blossom over a lean frame, and a late harvest
Deep colour for a white, from unusually thick skins
cards.a: A quiet grape that carries its site. Garganega ripens late, holds acidity, and gives almond, white blossom and a saline finish rather than obvious fruit. The best sites are the volcanic hills of Soave Classico; the flat land below is where the name was spent.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Taurasi in Campania is called the Barolo of the south. What does its Aglianico share with Nebbiolo?
options: A pale colour that browns within a few years
An aroma of tar and roses, from the same compounds
A refusal to grow anywhere outside its home hills
High acid over hard tannin, and a very late harvest
cards.a: The structure and the calendar. Aglianico holds high acidity over dense tannin and hangs into late October or November on volcanic slopes around Taurasi and Mount Vulture, so it needs years in bottle. It is far darker than Nebbiolo, which is the tell.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A wine smells clean in the glass, then leaves a stale, cereal, mouse-cage aftertaste. What happened?
options: Cork taint, which at low levels shows only on the palate
Mousiness, which only turns volatile at the pH of saliva
Oxidation, which the nose adapts to within a few seconds
The glass, holding detergent residue from a bad rinse
cards.a: The compounds behind it stay locked in a non-volatile form at wine's low pH and only become smellable once saliva raises the pH in your mouth. There is nothing to find in the glass. Dab a drop on the back of your hand and smell there. Roughly a third of people cannot perceive it.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Wine runs back down the inside of the glass in slow legs. What does that actually tell you?
options: Quality: a better wine leaves heavier, slower legs
Sugar, since sweetness is what thickens the film
Alcohol, because ethanol evaporates faster than water
Nothing at all, since it is a trick of the glass
cards.a: Ethanol evaporates faster than water, which raises surface tension in the film and drags wine up the wall until it beads and falls back. More alcohol, faster cycle. Glycerol adds a little viscosity and very little else. Legs are a rough alcohol reading, never a quality one.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One wine smells of vinegar and another of nail polish remover. Is that the same fault twice?
options: No: one is the acid, the other an ester made from it
Yes: both are volatile acidity at different strengths
No: the vinegar one is bacterial, the solvent one yeast
Yes, but the solvent note means it has gone further
cards.a: Linked but separate. Acetobacter needs oxygen and turns ethanol into acetic acid, which reads as vinegar somewhere around 600 to 900mg a litre. That acid then esterifies with ethanol into ethyl acetate, which reads as nail polish at about 12mg. You usually meet the ester first.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Wildfire smoke crossed a vineyard and the young wine tasted clean. Why can that change after bottling?
options: Oak ageing draws the smoke compounds back off the lees
It cannot: clean at bottling means clean for good
Bottling concentrates them, since nothing escapes the glass
The smoke compounds are bound to sugars and release slowly
cards.a: The vine defends itself by locking smoke phenols onto sugars, in which form they have no smell. Fermentation and then slow acid hydrolysis in bottle cut them loose, so an ashy, medicinal note can arrive months later. Filtering strips the free phenols but not the bound ones.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Opening sparkling wine, you hold the cork still and turn the bottle. Why that way round?
options: It keeps the label facing the guest throughout the pour
Turning the cork would snap it off inside the neck
The pressure is already pushing, so you only meter the rate
It stops the neck warming through the hand that holds it
cards.a: Five to six atmospheres sit behind that cork, several times a car tyre, and the bottle is doing the work of ejecting it. Gripping the cork and rotating the low-friction base means metering a cork that is already moving rather than fighting one. Keep a thumb over it throughout.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Wine goes out white before red, dry before sweet, young before old. What is that order protecting?
options: The glassware, since red leaves a film a rinse will not clear
Nothing measurable: it is a convention of the table
The temperature, since the cold bottles have to be poured first
The palate: tannin coats the mouth for a quarter of an hour
cards.a: Tannin binds and strips the proline-rich proteins in saliva, and the mouth takes eight to fifteen minutes to rebuild that film. Sugar masks in much the same way. So a tannic or sweet wine poured early flattens everything after it. Palate management, not etiquette.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A tasting exam marks you against a fixed word list rather than on whether your meaning was clear. Why?
options: So that two tasters anywhere describe one wine identically
To keep marking fast enough for a large cohort
Because plain description is too subjective to teach
To stop candidates naming the wine from its description
cards.a: A scale only works if everyone reads it the same way. Fixing the words to a set of scales makes one taster's note comparable with another's and with the key. The cost is that a near-miss word scores nothing, even where a person would have understood you perfectly.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Working blind toward a grape, a taster ranks clues by how far they can be trusted. What sits at the top?
options: Colour and clarity, being the least subjective to read
Oak and malolactic character, being the most obvious
Compounds the plant itself makes, like pepper or pyrazine
Alcohol, since it narrows the climate immediately
cards.a: Three tiers. A compound the plant carries is strongest: methoxypyrazine points at the Cabernet family, rotundone at Syrah, thiols at Sauvignon. Site clues such as acidity come next. Winemaking clues, oak and malolactic, are weakest, because anyone anywhere can choose them.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A ten pound bottle holds far more than twice the wine of a five pound one. What does that arithmetic?
options: Retail margin, which scales up with the shelf price
The fruit costs much the same, so only the oak differs
Cheap wine ships in bottle, which costs more per litre
Duty is a flat charge per bottle, so cheap wine has little left
cards.a: Excise is charged on alcohol, not on quality, so the same cash comes off both bottles. Add glass, closure, shipping and everyone's margin, and a cheap bottle has almost nothing left for the liquid. Nearly every extra pound you spend goes into the wine itself.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A dark tea brick shows fungal growth through it. What separates the wanted kind from the ruinous kind?
options: Colour alone: gold is wanted, anything else is not
The species, whether it was grown on purpose, and its shape
Smell alone, since spoilage mould always smells sour
Depth: growth on the surface is safe, growth inside is not
cards.a: Three things together. Golden flowers are one specific fungus, deliberately grown under held warmth and damp, and appear as small firm gold granules right through the brick. Spoilage mould is uninvited, fuzzy, white, green or black, smells musty, and carries a real toxin risk.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A tea is sold as bought direct from the farmer. What has usually actually been cut out?
options: The wholesale market and the broker, but rarely the pooling
Nothing: it is a marketing phrase with no substance
The refining factory, so the tea arrives unfinished
The export licence, which is why such tea costs less
cards.a: Usually the anonymous wholesale layer and the middlemen, not the pooling itself. The contact is often still a village station gathering several growers' leaf. Real single-farm buying exists at the top end, but nothing certifies the claim the way an organic label is certified.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Masala chai is boiled with its spices rather than steeped like tea. What forces that method?
options: The milk, which will not take up tea flavour below boiling
The spices: bark and seed give up nothing to a short steep
The leaf, which is too coarse to open in still water
Habit, since the tea in it brews perfectly well steeped
cards.a: Different materials give up at different rates. Cardamom, cinnamon bark, ginger and clove hold their oils in woody tissue a three minute steep barely touches, so they need a rolling boil and time. The tea is picked to survive that, which is why it is usually hard CTC.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A blender puts several different teas in one packet. Why do their leaf sizes usually match?
options: Different sizes give up at different rates, so the cup shifts
It looks uniform, and buyers reject a mixed-looking packet
Machines cannot fill a packet evenly with mixed sizes
Customs grades a blend by its smallest fraction
cards.a: Surface area sets extraction speed. Put fine broken leaf beside whole leaf and the small is spent inside a minute, while the large is still opening. The cup keeps changing shape as it brews, so no single time is right for it. Blenders match the grade first, then the flavour.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: A blend that tastes right at home comes out thin and dull a few hundred miles away. What is likely different?
options: The packaging, which has lost its seal in transit
The altitude, which has lowered the boiling point
The water, and the blend was built for the water at home
The shelf life, since blends stale faster than single teas
cards.a: Blenders build to the water their customers actually have. A blend pitched for hard, alkaline water is made brisk and strong so the minerals have something to knock down. Brewed in soft water that same leaf reads harsh; a soft-water blend in hard water goes flat.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Chrysanthemum, kuding and roasted barley are all sold as cha. What do they share with tea, chemically?
options: The polyphenols, which every plant infusion carries
The astringency, which is tannin in every one of them
The caffeine, which is what makes them all stimulating
Almost nothing: no caffeine, no theanine, no catechins
cards.a: Only the hot water. They come from unrelated families and carry none of tea's defining chemistry, so nothing you know about steeping tea transfers reliably. Each has its own extraction rate, its own kind of bitterness, and its own ways of going wrong.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Chrysanthemum is drunk alongside shou puerh far more often than on its own. What does the pairing do?
options: Its light florals lift a dark tea's heavy, earthy body
The flowers sweeten a tea that is otherwise bitter
It adds tannin, which gives the tea more grip
It slows the caffeine, so the tea can be drunk late
cards.a: Contrast. Shou puerh is thick, earthy and short on aromatic lift; chrysanthemum brings a clean floral top note and a little sweetness with almost no body of its own. Good flowers are picked before they fully open and dried whole, so a bag of loose petals is a poor sign.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Kuding is sold as a single famously bitter Chinese infusion. What is actually in the packet?
options: One plant, a holly, grown across several provinces
Young tea leaves, picked before the bitterness fades
Either a holly or a privet, two unrelated plants
A blend of bitter herbs, mixed to a fixed recipe
cards.a: Two different plants share the name: a holly sold as long dark twisted spears, and a privet sold as small flat leaves. They taste and behave differently. The bitterness is not tea's either, so cutting the steep short does not soften it the way it would a green.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: Monk fruit sweetens an infusion powerfully and adds almost no sugar. What is doing that?
options: Fructose, concentrated by drying the fruit very hard
A trace of stevia, added to the fruit during drying
Glycyrrhizin, the same compound that sweetens liquorice
Mogrosides, which the tongue reads as intensely sweet
cards.a: Mogrosides, a group of compounds the fruit builds that read as sweet far below the concentration sugar needs, while carrying almost no energy. They hold up to boiling, which is why luo han guo is simmered into soups and cough syrups rather than only steeped.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Hunter Valley Semillon is picked early, sees no oak and goes into bottle at about 11%. Why does it then age for decades?
options: The low alcohol slows every reaction in the bottle
High acid and no oak leave nothing to fall away first
Thick skins carry tannin, which acts as a preservative
It is sealed under a closure that admits no oxygen at all
cards.a: Picked before the sugar builds, it holds very high acid and almost no primary fruit, so a young one tastes thin and neutral. Nothing is laid over it and nothing is waiting to drop out. A decade in bottle builds toast, honey and lanolin out of the wine itself.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Margaret River sits on a peninsula with ocean on three sides of it. What does that buy its Cabernet?
options: A narrow temperature range, so ripening runs slow and even
Salt carried inland, which is the region's savoury signature
Constant wind, which thickens the skins as they grow
Rain right through ripening, which swells the berries
cards.a: Maritime moderation. Water warms and cools slowly, so the swing between day and night, and between one month and the next, is unusually small and the fruit ripens gradually. Cabernet finishes there without the baked, jammy edge a hot inland site gives it.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Tasmania is too cool to ripen most of what Australia is known for. What has it become instead?
options: A Riesling region, since Riesling wants the coolest sites
The source of most of Australia's premium sparkling base
A sweet wine region, using the very long hang time
A nursery, raising rootstock for the mainland to plant
cards.a: Base wine for sparkling. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir grown that cool arrive high in acid and low in sugar, which is wrong for a still wine and right for a second fermentation. The island also makes still Pinot that reads far closer to Burgundy than the mainland does.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: McLaren Vale's oldest Grenache stands as unirrigated bushes on deep sand. Why is that fruit now sought after?
options: Sand holds the day's heat, which is what ripens Grenache
The vines were planted for fortified wine, which wants old wood
Bush training shades the fruit, which keeps the colour pale
No water and poor sand force tiny crops of concentrated fruit
cards.a: Dry-grown old bush vines on deep sand carry very little fruit and root a long way down for water, so the berries come in small and concentrated. Grenache was planted here for fortified wine and nearly pulled out when that market died. What survived makes the region's best reds.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: South Africa holds more Chenin Blanc than anywhere on earth, and most of it was planted for brandy. What changed?
options: A clonal programme replaced the old plant material entirely
Growers found the old dry-grown bush vines make serious wine
The climate cooled enough for Chenin to hold its acidity
The law changed to admit Chenin into the top appellations
cards.a: Nothing in the vineyard. Chenin, called Steen there, went in by the thousand hectares for distilling and bulk, much of it old, dry-grown bush vine on poor ground. Once anyone troubled to crop it low and ferment it in barrel it turned out to make world-class white.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: The Cape sits at a latitude that ought to be far too hot for fine wine. What holds it in balance?
options: Cold Atlantic water, and the wind that comes in off it
Altitude, since almost every vineyard sits above 1000m
Cloud cover across the whole of the growing season
A short season, so fruit is picked before the real heat
cards.a: Cold water, and the wind off it. The Benguela current runs up the west coast out of the Southern Ocean, and the south-easter blows off it all summer, the wind locals call the Cape Doctor. How near a vineyard sits to that water shapes its style more than its latitude.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Sancerre's growers name three different soils and price the wines by which one. What do those soils actually change?
options: The colour, since flint noticeably darkens a white wine
How fast the site drains, and so how taut the wine reads
The permitted yield, which the appellation sets by soil
Nothing measurable: the names are a marketing habit
cards.a: Drainage. Marl holds water and gives the broadest, slowest-maturing wine; limestone gravel drains hard and gives the most aromatic; flint drains hardest and gives the tautest, with the smoky note growers call gunflint. Pouilly-Fume sits across the river on the same seam.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: On Santorini the vines are woven flat into low coiled baskets on the ground. What is that shape for?
options: Keeping fruit off soil that would otherwise scorch it
Concentrating heat, since the island is barely warm enough
Making the harvest possible without ladders on the terraces
Shelter from the wind, and catching the night's sea mist
cards.a: Wind and water. The island is scoured by the meltemi, its summer wind, and gets almost no rain. So the vine is trained into a coiled basket, a kouloura. The fruit sits inside it, sheltered from wind and sun, and the basket gathers dew off the night mist.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Naoussa's Xinomavro pours pale, browns young and grips hard. Which far better known grape does that describe?
options: Nebbiolo, which shares the pale colour and the hard tannin
Pinot Noir, which is equally pale and equally fragile
Syrah, which also browns early in a warm vintage
Sangiovese, which has the same high acid and light colour
cards.a: Nebbiolo, and the resemblance is close enough that tasters mistake the two blind. The name means acid black: high acidity over dense tannin with very little pigment, and a tomato and dried-herb character. It wants years, and Naoussa in Macedonia is its home.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Oregon's Willamette Valley is the New World region most often set beside Burgundy. What makes the comparison fair?
options: The soils, which are the same limestone as the Cote d'Or
A cool, marine-influenced climate, with rain at harvest
The clones, brought out of Burgundy in the 1960s
Its latitude, which is identical to that of Beaune
cards.a: Not the rock but the weather. The valley lies open to the Pacific through a gap in the Coast Range, so it is cool, cloudy and wet. Vintage genuinely matters there, and rot is a live threat. That marginality, rather than the soil, is what it shares with Burgundy.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Washington grows most of its wine in near-desert east of the Cascades, on eight inches of rain a year. How does that work?
options: The vines are dry-farmed, and the drought concentrates them
Every vineyard is irrigated, so water becomes a dial
Winter snowmelt soaks the soil deeply enough to last
The fruit is picked early, before the drought can bite
cards.a: Irrigation turns a liability into control. With almost no rain, a grower decides exactly when the vine gets water and when it goes short, which is a lever growers in wetter places do not have. The sandy soils also carry no phylloxera, so much of the state is ungrafted.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Some of Sonoma's coolest vineyards lie south of its warmest. What breaks the usual rule that south means warmer?
options: Fog and cold air drawn inland through gaps in the hills
Altitude, since the southern sites all sit much higher
The soils, which hold cold water through the summer
Tree cover, which shades the southern vineyards
cards.a: Where the coast range breaks. Cold Pacific air and fog pour through gaps such as the Petaluma Gap and up the Russian River. So a site's distance from an opening decides its temperature more than its latitude. Two vineyards an hour apart can be different climates.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Chile spent over a century growing what it believed was Merlot. What did DNA testing find in 1994?
options: It was a Chilean crossing, unrelated to anything French
Much of it was Carmenere, a Bordeaux grape thought extinct
It was Cabernet Franc, misidentified at the nursery
It was Merlot, but a mutation unique to the country
cards.a: Carmenere, a Bordeaux variety phylloxera had all but wiped out in France. It ripens a good two weeks after Merlot, so picking the mixed rows on Merlot's schedule left it green and pyrazine-heavy. Given its own harvest date it comes in dark, savoury and soft.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Rueda sits on the high Castilian plateau of northern Spain, where summer days are fierce. How does its Verdejo stay fresh?
options: The grape is picked well before it is fully ripe
Acid is added, which the appellation permits in Rueda
It is fermented cold enough to hold its acidity in
Altitude and cold nights, and picking through the night
cards.a: Height and the dark. Vineyards sit around 700 to 800m, so nights fall hard even in August and the fruit holds acidity. Most of the crop is machine-picked overnight to bring it in cold, because Verdejo oxidises readily. It gives a bitter-almond finish that is its signature.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Hermitage is one granite hill of about 130 hectares. Why is that hill worth more than the flat land beside it?
options: It turns to face due south, where the valley runs north
It is the only granite in the whole northern Rhone
The river bends around it, which keeps frost away
It escaped phylloxera, so its vines are far older
cards.a: Aspect. The Rhone runs roughly north to south, so its slopes mostly face east or west. At Tain the hill swings round and presents a broad south face to the sun. At this latitude that is what finishes Syrah. Cote-Rotie is the same trick on a smaller scale.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Provence, on France's Mediterranean coast, makes rose as its main product rather than a by-product. What does that change in the vineyard?
options: Nothing: rose is decided at the press, not in the vineyard
Fruit is grown and picked for pink, so it comes in earlier
Only white grapes are planted, and colour is added later
Yields are pushed high, since colour does not matter
cards.a: The decision moves back to the vine. Where rose is the plan, growers pick earlier, for acidity and pale colour, not the phenolic ripeness a red needs. Sites and varieties are chosen for it too. A rose bled off a red ferment comes from fruit picked for something else.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Touriga Nacional is Portugal's most prized red grape, and growers still plant very little of it. Why?
options: It is legally capped, to protect the traditional blends
It has no resistance to the region's fungal diseases
It ripens too late for anywhere outside the Douro
It crops so lightly that it barely pays on its own
cards.a: Yield. Left alone it sets a tiny crop of small, thick-skinned berries. That is exactly why the wine is so dark and perfumed, and exactly why a grower paid by weight avoids it. It anchors Port blends and, on the granite of the Dao, makes floral, firm dry reds.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: A shelf holds Montepulciano d'Abruzzo beside Vino Nobile di Montepulciano. Are these related?
options: No: one names a grape, the other a Tuscan town
Yes: the same grape, grown in two different regions
Yes: one is the younger release of the other
No: one is red and the other is a dried-grape sweet wine
cards.a: A pure coincidence of names. Montepulciano is a grape, grown mostly in Abruzzo on the Adriatic side, giving deep, soft, low-acid red. Vino Nobile comes from the hill town of Montepulciano in Tuscany and is made from Sangiovese. Nothing connects them but the word.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Alto Adige is Italy's most northerly wine region, deep in the Alps, and most of its output is white. Why whites there?
options: The reds were pulled out after a run of failed vintages
Steep, high, cold sites hold the acidity whites need
Italian law reserves the region's slopes for white grapes
The soils are too poor to ripen any red variety at all
cards.a: Altitude and aspect in an Alpine valley. Vineyards climb past 1000m on steep sides, so nights are cold and the season long, which is what aromatic whites want. Pinot Grigio and Gewurztraminer are taken seriously here in a way they are not further south.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Sauternes, upriver of Bordeaux, gets reliable noble rot almost every year while its neighbours do not. What does it have that they lack?
options: A warmer microclimate, which the fungus needs to spread
A cold tributary meeting a warm river, which makes autumn mist
Soils that hold water, keeping the bunches damp overnight
A later-ripening clone, so the fruit hangs into the mists
cards.a: A river junction. The cold Ciron runs into the warmer Garonne, and the temperature difference throws up mist most autumn mornings that burns off by afternoon. Damp then dry is exactly the cycle botrytis needs; stay wet and the same fungus becomes grey rot.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Pessac-Leognan is the only corner of Bordeaux ranked for its whites as well as its reds. Why there?
options: It is the coolest part of Bordeaux, which whites need
Gravel that suits Cabernet sits beside sand and clay that suit whites
Its chateaux were excluded from 1855 and needed a rank of their own
White grapes are barred from the rest of the Left Bank
cards.a: Mixed ground in one place. The same deep gravel that finishes Cabernet runs beside patches of sand and clay where Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon do well, so estates make both seriously. The 1959 Graves list ranks them for each colour separately.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Pomerol holds some of the most expensive wine on earth and has no classification at all. How does a buyer navigate it?
options: By name and by soil, since reputation does the work a rank would
By vintage, since the appellation is too small to vary by estate
By the Saint-Emilion list, which Pomerol estates may join
By alcohol, which the best sites reach and the rest do not
cards.a: Reputation, unranked. It is tiny, there is no list and no tasting panel, so the market simply prices what it trusts. Soil does much of it: a seam of dense clay under part of the plateau holds water for Merlot in a dry year, and the estates sitting on it are the famous ones.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: The Cote de Nuits is almost entirely red and the great white grand crus all sit in the Cote de Beaune. What splits them?
options: A rule: white grapes may not be planted in the Cote de Nuits
The Nuits is warmer, and Chardonnay needs the cooler half
The ground changes, and growers followed it with the grape
The Beaune was replanted to white after phylloxera
cards.a: Geology, followed by habit. Marl heavy in clay and limestone runs through the southern half in bands that suit Chardonnay, while the Nuits sits on ground where Pinot Noir has long done better. Nothing forbids either grape; four centuries of growers simply settled it.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: The Maconnais makes Chardonnay at a fraction of Cote de Beaune prices, from the same grape. What is different?
options: The grape is a different clone, bred for volume
It is machine-harvested, which the Cote d'Or forbids
It may be chaptalised, which the Cote d'Or may not
It lies further south and lower, so the wine is riper and rounder
cards.a: Latitude and lie. Southern Burgundy is warmer and its slopes gentler, so Chardonnay ripens more easily and gives a broader, softer, earlier-drinking wine. Pouilly-Fuisse holds the best sites, and it finally got premier crus of its own in 2020.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: One Chinon is light and crunchy, the next firm enough to cellar. Both are Cabernet Franc. What separates them?
options: The ground: river gravel against the limestone of the slopes
The vintage, since only warm years give the firmer wine
Whole-bunch fermentation, used only for the firmer style
Vine age, since only old vines give enough tannin
cards.a: Where on the valley it grew. Gravel terraces by the Vienne warm fast and give the light, floral, chill-it style. The tuffeau limestone slopes above hold water and ripen slower, giving structure and the graphite edge that lets a Chinon run twenty years.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Gigondas sits above Cotes du Rhone in the southern ladder, on the same Grenache. What earns the step up?
options: A longer minimum ageing before the wine may be released
A ban on white grapes, which Cotes du Rhone permits
Higher, cooler ground under the Dentelles, and a lower yield
Hand harvesting, which the lower tier does not require
cards.a: Site and crop. The vineyards climb the limestone teeth of the Dentelles de Montmirail, so nights fall cooler than on the plain and the fruit keeps acidity. The cru caps yields well below the regional appellation, and the wine comes out firmer and longer.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: In the Alentejo some wine is still fermented and kept in tall clay jars sunk into the floor. What does the clay do?
options: Nothing: it is a tradition kept for the look of the cellar
It insulates so well that the wine ferments without cooling
It leaches minerals, which is the style's savoury signature
It breathes a little, like a barrel, but adds no flavour of its own
cards.a: Slow air and no wood. Unlined clay lets a trace of oxygen through the wall much as a cask does, so the wine softens. But it contributes no vanilla, no toast and no tannin of its own. Vinho de Talha became a protected category in 2010, reviving a Roman practice.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Santa Barbara grows cool-climate Pinot Noir further south than Los Angeles. How is that possible?
options: Its valleys run east to west, funnelling cold ocean air inland
Altitude, since the vineyards all sit high in the mountains
Persistent cloud, which sits over the county all summer
Irrigation with cold water drawn from deep aquifers
cards.a: The mountains lie the wrong way, and it is a gift. Almost the whole American coast runs north to south, but the transverse ranges here run east to west, opening the Santa Ynez and Santa Maria valleys straight to the Pacific. Cold air and fog pour in, and it gets warmer inland.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: The Finger Lakes grow Riesling at a latitude where winter can kill a vine outright. What makes it survivable?
options: The vines are buried each autumn and dug out in spring
Riesling is simply hardy enough to take the winters
Deep glacial lakes hold heat and keep the worst cold off
Snow cover insulates the vineyards through the coldest months
cards.a: The water. The lakes are deep enough not to freeze, so they give back stored warmth through the winter and hold the air above the shore above the killing point. They also delay budbreak in spring, which keeps the vine out of the frost. Slopes furthest from water are the riskiest.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Riesling is among the greatest white grapes and is almost never put in new oak. Why not?
options: Its skins react with oak tannin and the wine turns bitter
German law forbids new oak for Riesling above a set level
The wine is bottled too young for oak to have any effect
Its aromas are delicate, and its acid needs no softening
cards.a: There is nothing for oak to do and plenty for it to bury. Riesling's lift comes from light aromatic compounds that vanilla and toast smother, and its acidity is the point rather than a problem to round off. Where wood is used it is old and large, so it breathes without flavouring.

cards.subject: tea
cards.q: What makes a Wuyi tea a rock oolong, rather than just an oolong that happens to grow at Wuyi?
options: The cultivar, since only a few named bushes qualify
A minimum oxidation level, set by the county
Where it grew in the cliffs, and a heavy charcoal roast
Three years of ageing before it may be sold
cards.a: Two things together: the ground and the fire. Yancha means rock tea, off the eroded cliffs and ravines of the Wuyi mountains in northern Fujian, and the style is finished by charcoal roasting repeated over months. Da Hong Pao, Rou Gui and Shui Xian are the names you meet.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Santorini's vines are among the oldest in Europe and not one of them is grafted. Why has phylloxera never taken hold?
options: The island was quarantined before the louse could reach it
The heat, which kills the louse in the top of the soil
The sea, since the louse cannot cross open water
Volcanic sand, which the root louse cannot move through
cards.a: The ground. Phylloxera cannot move through pure sand, so the island never needed American rootstock. Vines grow on their own roots. They are renewed by bending a cane back into the soil to root, so one plant can be centuries old while its wood stays young.

cards.subject: wine
cards.q: Barbera and Dolcetto grow side by side in Piedmont and are easy to confuse. Which is which in the glass?
options: Barbera has the firm tannin, Dolcetto the sharp acid
Both run high in acid, and only the colour separates them
Barbera has the sharp acid, Dolcetto the firm tannin
Both are soft, and Barbera is simply the darker of the two
cards.a: They are opposites. Barbera pours dark and juicy, high in acid over soft tannin, so it drinks young. Dolcetto is the reverse: low acid with firm, faintly bitter tannin, and its name, little sweet one, points at that soft acidity. It ripens weeks earlier than Nebbiolo too.
